| the answer of the next row of the same question type | 0 / 491 / 193 | 0 / 684 / 0 |
| the answer with its first number raised by 1 | 0 / 533 / 151 | 0 / 684 / 0 |

- **Phase tags.** With the `convert_hardmath` contracts 562 calls reach the deadline over all the replies I graded, and all of them report `phase: comparison`. None is a reference parse, so none of them counts toward the block.
- **`convert_hardmath_rhs`.** None of its 7,319 calls reaches the deadline, and the slowest takes 2.75 s. The wrong replies score 0: the two in the table, the last number raised by 1, a changed exponent, the first member alone, and exchanged members. The exceptions have the reference's value: 34 integral rows whose two members are the same text, and 3 integral rows whose reference has the coefficient `0.00`.
- **`polynomial_roots`, 65 rows.** The dataset writes these answers as `\left[…\right], \left[…\right]`. `convert_hardmath` grades that text as one SCALAR. `convert_hardmath_rhs` puts it inside `[` and `]` and grades a LIST of two members. A reply in the dataset's form then scores 0 on all 65 rows: `_split_members` removes the reply's first `[` and last `]` as if they enclosed the whole text, and the reply splits into three members. The golden control carries the outer brackets and scores 1, so admission does not show this. On main the same split scores `(1,2),(3,4)` 0 against the LIST reference `[(1,2),(3,4)]`.
- **Regrouped answers.** For symbolic nondimensionalization, the regrouping `\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{p/q}}{a_{2}^{p/q} a_{3}}` of my earlier comment scores 0 on 89 of 89 rows with `convert_hardmath_rhs`. With `convert_hardmath` it reaches the deadline on 74 and scores 0 on 15.

Row 122 of the train split, with its own answer text as the reply:

```python
from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

answer = r"\left[ - \sqrt{\frac{1.00}{\epsilon}}, \  \sqrt{\frac{1.00}{\epsilon}}\right], \left[ \frac{1.00}{\epsilon}, \  -1.00\right]"
print(grade_math_candidate(MathSpec(expected=answer, math_type=MathType.SCALAR), answer).reward)
print(grade_math_candidate(MathSpec(expected=f"[{answer}]", math_type=MathType.LIST), answer).reward)
print(grade_math_candidate(MathSpec(expected=f"[{answer}]", math_type=MathType.LIST), f"[{answer}]").reward)
```

It prints `1.0`, `0.0` and `1.0`. The first contract is the one `convert_hardmath` builds for this row and the other two use the one `convert_hardmath_rhs` builds.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 The `_split_members` false negative is fixed on main and on `atlas-env-audit`, and the HARDMath RHS release re-grades clean.

**The fix.** `_split_members` dropped a sequence's first and last characters whenever they read as an opener/closer pair by type, so a reply whose members carry their own brackets lost one bracket per side and split into broken members. It now strips the outer layer only when the first opener's balanced close is the last character, and otherwise splits the top level as is. PR on main: #11739 (row-122 and `(1,2),(3,4)`-vs-`[(1,2),(3,4)]` regression tests included, both verified failing before the fix; full verifyit suite green). Landed on `atlas-env-audit` via atlas-push at 91ebdc65fe (1,536 verifyit tests green on the rebased head).

**Re-grade of the HARDMath RHS release** (684 converted rows of `pafitis/HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10` under the `convert_hardmath_rhs` contracts at the landed head; every call through `verifyit.grade.run` in its own process; cells are rows scored 1 / scored 0 / at the deadline):

| reply | scored 1 | scored 0 | deadline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| the contract's own reference | 684 | 0 | 0 |
| the dataset's answer text | 684 | 0 | 0 |
| the answer of the next converted row | 0 | 684 | 0 |
| the contract reference with its first number raised by 1 | 0 | 684 | 0 |

The dataset's answer text was 619/65/0 under the bug; the 65 `polynomial_roots` false negatives are gone and the wrong replies still score 0. None of the 2,736 calls reaches the deadline and the slowest takes 1.27 s; all 65 `polynomial_roots` rows score 1 on the dataset's own form.

**Receipt impact.** No receipt of the RHS release computed a reward under the bug: conversion receipts validate references only (the reference `[\left[…\right], \left[…\right]]` split correctly even under the bug — that is why admission missed this), the retained census is a static conversion census, the lexical scan is text-only, and the retained-release receipt, fingerprint index and license receipt bind identity, not grades. No difficulty-campaign trial tree exists anywhere under `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas/difficulty` for the rhs source hash `83371b10…`, and no SAMPLE QC ran for the variant, so no difficulty measurement or admission receipt needs re-measuring. The only record the bug corrupted is the replay table in the comment above (619/65/0), which this table supersedes. Nothing deleted, nothing re-registered.

**The 89 symbolic-nondimensionalization regroupings** score 0 because math-verify's equivalence check is conservative, not because of a contract bug. The regrouping `\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{p/q}}{a_{3}}` → `\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{p/q}}{a_{2}^{p/q} a_{3}}` parses on both sides; SymPy cannot prove the identity without positivity assumptions (`simplify` leaves a nonzero difference), and proves it exactly with `positive=True` symbols. The dataset's coefficients are positive, so the regrouped reply is semantically right and loses the point — a false negative of the verifier's exactness, never a false positive. Examples (row → reference → regrouped reply, all scoring 0):

- row 9: `\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{3}}` → `\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{19}{9}} a_{3}}`
- row 20: `\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{17}{6}}}{a_{3}}` → `\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{17}{6}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{17}{6}} a_{3}}`
- row 29: `\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{5}{4}}}{a_{3}}` → `\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{5}{4}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{5}{4}} a_{3}}`

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A symbolic math reply that is equal to the reference only under positivity assumptions scores 0, because math-verify's comparison cannot prove the identity for unassumed symbols. The grader never awards a false positive here — the failure mode is a conservative false negative on an equivalent answer. On the HARDMath mirror (`pafitis/HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10`), 89 of 89 symbolic-nondimensionalization rows whose reference carries a power of a ratio score 0 when the reply regroups the same expression into a ratio of powers (89 of the 101 `nondimensionalization_symbolic` rows have that form; measured through `verifyit.grade.run` under the `convert_hardmath_rhs` contracts, replay in [#11511 (comment)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11511#issuecomment-7006269885)). This is independent of the member-splitting bug fixed in #11739.

Reproduce:
1. Grade a regrouped reply against its reference with the symbolic math grader:

    ```python
    from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
    from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

    # HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10, question_type nondimensionalization_symbolic
    cases = [
        (r"\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{3}}",
         r"\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{19}{9}} a_{3}}"),  # row 9
        (r"\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{17}{6}}}{a_{3}}",
         r"\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{17}{6}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{17}{6}} a_{3}}"),  # row 20
        (r"\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{5}{4}}}{a_{3}}",
         r"\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{5}{4}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{5}{4}} a_{3}}"),    # row 29
    ]
    for reference, reply in cases:
        spec = MathSpec(expected=reference, math_type=MathType.SCALAR)
        print(grade_math_candidate(spec, reply).reward)  # 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    ```

2. Each row prints 0.0; the reference itself, the reply form with the outer ratio kept, and wrong replies grade normally, so the 0 comes from the comparison of two parsed expressions, not from a parse failure.

Expected: the regrouped reply grades 1.0. It equals the reference wherever the coefficients are positive, and these datasets' coefficients are positive constants (for example `1.00`); a silent 0 for a semantically correct answer shape undercounts measured solve rates for any source whose answers contain powers of ratios.

Confirmed root cause of the 0: both sides parse to expressions, and the equality needs positivity. Row 9 parses to `a_1*(a_3/a_2)**(19/9)/a_3` (reference) and `a_1*a_3**(19/9)/(a_2**(19/9)*a_3)` (reply); `sympy.simplify(gold - target)` without assumptions leaves a nonzero difference, and the same simplify with the symbols declared `positive=True` returns exactly 0.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The reported regrouping parses on both sides, but `math_verify.verify` compares symbols without the positivity needed to prove the identity. VerifyIt has no domain assumptions in `MathSpec`; the shared task converter constructs that spec without source-specific symbol metadata. A global positive-symbol rule would change scores for tasks with unrestricted variables (for example, `\sqrt{x^2}` versus `x` at negative `x`).

**Relevant code**
- [`grade_math.py#L106-L155`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L106-L155) — symbolic comparison
- [`grade_math.py#L367-L405`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L367-L405) — candidate scoring
- [`spec.py#L143-L149`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/spec.py#L143-L149) — math contract fields
- [`answers.py#L108-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/convert/answers.py#L108-L123) — shared spec construction
- [`math.py#L209-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/math.py#L209-L215) — HARDMath conversion on main

# Proposed Fix

1. Audit the 89 affected `nondimensionalization_symbolic` questions in `pafitis/HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10` for an explicit positive domain for each symbolic coefficient. The presence of positive numeric constants alone does not establish the domain of every symbol. Record any exceptions and leave those contracts unchanged.
2. Add an opt-in tuple of positive symbol names to `MathSpec`, defaulting to empty. After ordinary scalar comparison fails, substitute positive SymPy symbols on both parsed expressions and retry an exact, deadline-bounded comparison. Keep equations, sets, and the default grading policy unchanged; validate names and reject malformed contracts.
3. Pass the assumption only from a HARDMath conversion whose audited question establishes it. Coordinate this with the RHS-only HARDMath contract on the `atlas-env-audit` integration branch; main currently converts the whole `ground_truths` field.
4. Add public-API regressions for the three reported regroupings, a wrong exponent, and `\sqrt{x^2}` versus `x` with and without an explicit positive `x`. Replay all 89 affected rows and wrong-answer controls through `verifyit.grade.run`; accept the change only if the supported regroupings score 1, wrong replies remain 0, and no calls reach the deadline. The implementation PR should use `Fixes #11740`.

This spans the grader contract, shared conversion, and an audited dataset release, so it needs a scoped implementation rather than a global comparator change.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The LOCAL route's disk guardian repeatedly fails to set up its loop device on CoreWeave CPU workers, losing the trial as infrastructure before the machine starts:

```
RuntimeError: mount failed: mount: /tmp/<work-root>/worker/sandbox-disks/sandbox-6oc8r1nb/data:
  failed to setup loop device for /tmp/<work-root>/worker/sandbox-disks/sandbox-6oc8r1nb/disk.img.
```

Observed in `/benfeuer/atlas-repair-nl2bash-campaign-sample50-v1` (4 of 50 trials, all attempt-00/01/02 across retries; the sibling trials on the same worker ran the same disk path shape successfully, so the capacity appears to be per-worker loop-device headroom rather than a config error). The same campaign shape (`--environment local`, one sparse `storage_mb` disk per machine, up to 4 concurrent trials plus their verifiers) completed 372 rows on another worker the day before.

Impact: every trial that hits the exhausted loop-device budget dies as `Local disk guardian failed; allocation retained for startup recovery`, and the campaign burns its retries on a resource the scheduler does not account for.

Possible directions: surface loop-device availability in the worker's capacity/accounting before acquiring a trial, detach stale loop devices under the disk root before failing, or fail the allocation with a retryable provider error that does not consume the trial's attempt budget.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

The LOCAL disk path is in open PR #11277. Its pool probes one loop mount at construction, but each later sandbox mount obtains a loop device without capacity admission; the reported `mount` error occurs before the machine starts. A worker snapshot is needed to distinguish live device saturation from an abandoned attachment or missing device access.

Relevant code: [`disk.py` allocation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/91ebdc65fe2f369d9f1109164038ad2cece7ed70/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/disk.py#L186-L212), [`disk_lifecycle.py` mount and scoped reclaim](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/91ebdc65fe2f369d9f1109164038ad2cece7ed70/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/disk_lifecycle.py#L31-L70), [oracle infrastructure attempt budget](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/91ebdc65fe2f369d9f1109164038ad2cece7ed70/experiments/post_training/task_curation/oracle_filter.py#L1027-L1036).

**Proposed Fix**

1. Capture `losetup -a`, visible `/dev/loop*` devices, mount namespace, disk-root mounts, and guardian leases on an affected worker while the failure is present. Confirm whether the limit is shared across worker pods and how many disks each trial and verifier holds.
2. If live allocations exhaust the devices, gate LOCAL dispatch on a host-wide loop-device budget that includes verifier disks and holds each slot through guardian cleanup. If abandoned attachments are the cause, reclaim only loop devices backed by released leases under that disk root. Keep the existing live-lease protection.
3. Classify a loop-allocation failure that races admission as provider capacity unavailable before charging a trial attempt. Add a regression for concurrent trials and verifiers at the measured device limit, plus a privileged-worker check that leases and loop devices return to baseline after teardown.

The fix should land in #11277's stack; a separate PR now would overlap the open implementation.

The shellbox LOCAL machine that runs a converted workspace task's grader environment comes up with no working DNS, so any grader whose declared setup calls `apt-get update` fails and every such trial is lost as infrastructure. The declared verifier network policy (`allow`) is not applied: the trial's network-policy receipt records `verifier_declared: "allow"` but `verifier_effective: null`.

Reproduce (2 nl2bash rows from the sealed repair-lane cohort):

3. Both trials fail in the grader environment setup. The captured setup stdout begins `Ign:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble InRelease ...` and ends `Err:1 ... Temporary failure resolving 'archive.ubuntu.com'` for all four noble repos, then `E: Unable to locate package build-essential`, `E: Package 'ca-certificates' has no installation candidate`, and the same for `python3-pip`, `python3-venv`, `tmux`, `unzip`, `vim`, `wget` (exit 100).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The current Atlas trial adapter passes the source verifier network policy into the grader `MachineSpec`, but records `verifier_effective` only after machine creation returns. The reported `null` receipt therefore does not establish that `allow` was ignored; it needs to be reconciled with the grader setup output and the executor revision. Shellbox copies the host resolver configuration for host-backed machines, while its OCI image creation path prepares apt without an equivalent resolver step. That is a plausible cause of the DNS failure, pending a check of the failed grader's `/etc/resolv.conf`.

**Relevant code**
- [TaskSpec trial policy and receipt](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/91ebdc65fe2f369d9f1109164038ad2cece7ed70/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/taskcompendium.py#L219-L229) — records policy after creation.

# Proposed Fix

1. For one failed LOCAL trial, record the executor commit, grader image digest, final `network-policy.json`, grader `/etc/resolv.conf`, host `/etc/resolv.conf`, and a DNS probe from the same grader image. Check whether the `null` receipt came from machine creation, a different executor revision, or artifact persistence.
2. Reproduce with the pinned grader image under LOCAL `network=allow`. If its resolver is missing or unusable, supply a working resolver in Shellbox's OCI machine root and add a behavioral regression for DNS with `allow` and isolation with `deny`.
3. Rerun the two nl2bash controls through the same LOCAL route. Require successful declared apt setup and `verifier_effective: "allow"` in both receipts before replaying the larger cohort.

[PR #11277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11277) already owns the TaskSpec trial adapter and independent actor/verifier policy wiring, so any adapter change should land there; a Shellbox resolver fix can be scoped separately after the probe confirms it.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
`marina apps table load` stages rows as 250-row INSERT batches through the applet SQL gateway (`infra/marina/src/marina/table_load.py`, `INSERT_BATCH_ROWS = 250`). There is no server-side bulk path (COPY, staged parquet ingestion, or a released-job runner) for large app datasets.

Impact: any app load beyond a small dataset drives thousands of gateway statements. During the RL Data Atlas preview reload (a 320-source serving catalog, ~51,000 item rows and the retained-assessment carry-forward), the sustained statement stream crashed the shared Cloud Run gateway with 503s ("The service you requested is not available at this time", service error -27) while production shared the same deployment. The gateway's 10-second per-statement guard (`QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS = 10000` in `infra/marina/src/marina/applets.py`) also rejects legitimate statements: per-pipeline retained-copy INSERT..SELECTs over ~150,000 indexed rows, and batched item inserts spiking past 10 seconds under contention on a table carrying ~2.4 million retained rows plus four indexes including a GIN index.

Observed events (2026-11-18): repeated 504 statement timeouts during the staged load; one 503 gateway crash mid-load; the load aborted without selecting. The Atlas loader already bounds everything it can locally (per-table byte budgets, row-count caps, per-pipeline and per-bucket carry-forward copies, a deduplicated probe through materialized summaries) — the remaining constraint is the transport, not the statements.

Options:
1. The apps tooling gains a server-side bulk path: stage rows to object storage, one server-side COPY per table through the app's database role (the released-job runner or an ops-authorized maintenance connection).
2. The released-job runner (`marina.jobs.job_engine()`) runs load jobs inside the Marina runtime with direct database access — currently blocked on runner capacity in the infrastructure-owned runtime configuration.

Until one lands, large app loads can only use paced, resumable gateway drivers with retry-on-flap, which is fragile at this volume.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`apps table load` reads the full Arrow table, then sends one SQL request per 250-row batch. Atlas uses a separate loader but sends its batches through the same gateway. Each request gets a 10-second statement timeout; changing only `table_load.py` would leave the Atlas reload exposed. Released jobs already have an app-role database engine, but `runtime.toml` grants runner capacity only to Echo and EvalDash.

**Relevant code**
- [`table_load.py#L60-L88`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea1257ca8d7a968397f2493b968035c8eb1caa46/infra/marina/src/marina/table_load.py#L60-L88) — 250-row INSERT generation.
- [`cli.py#L599-L621`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea1257ca8d7a968397f2493b968035c8eb1caa46/infra/marina/src/marina/cli.py#L599-L621) — one gateway request per statement.
- [`applets.py#L1089-L1122`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea1257ca8d7a968397f2493b968035c8eb1caa46/infra/marina/src/marina/applets.py#L1089-L1122) — app role and 10-second guard.
- [`rl_data_catalog/load.py#L57-L95`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea1257ca8d7a968397f2493b968035c8eb1caa46/infra/marina/apps/rl_data_catalog/load.py#L57-L95) — Atlas gateway batches.
- [`jobs.py#L23-L51`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ea1257ca8d7a968397f2493b968035c8eb1caa46/infra/marina/src/marina/jobs.py#L23-L51) — direct app-role engine and runner limits.

# Proposed Fix

This needs a runtime and app-loader change, followed by a general table-loader change:

1. Add an on-demand bulk runner in `runtime.toml` and Pulumi, with explicit per-app permission, resource and time limits, and no scheduler trigger. Run released app modules through `job_engine()` so writes use the selected app's role. Keep the 10-second SQL gateway guard for interactive requests.
2. Move the Atlas import into a released job. Pin the source snapshot, stream row data to Postgres through the worker (probe the current driver for `COPY FROM STDIN`), run retained-copy SQL through the same direct connection, check counts, and switch `atlas_current` only after validation. A failed run must leave the previous snapshot selected and be safe to retry.
3. Add a bulk mode to `apps table load`: upload the input to an app-scoped regional object prefix, submit a bounded worker run using server-resolved app role and validated table name, stream into a staging table, then commit an append or atomic replacement. Track the staged object's digest and run status so a retry cannot duplicate rows; delete abandoned staging objects.

Done when an Atlas preview reload of the reported ~51,000 items against the indexed retained table completes without bulk SQL gateway traffic, the previous snapshot survives an injected load failure, and real-Postgres tests cover app-role isolation plus append, replace, and retry behavior. Record gateway request count, load duration, and row counts before enabling the path for production.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

On the 64-H100 Long Loop layout with XLA autotune level 0, EAGER CUDA module loading has not eliminated the intermittent first-step stall. On source `5cbfba9f`, both fresh-state expert-MuonH runs without a host rebind (G5 and G20) stalled on their first stock call; they were submitted 60 ms apart and shared fabric. In the recorded EAGER/autotune-0 BF16 cohort with host rebind, six first stock calls completed (v9, C-replay r3, C-e12, G5r2, G20r2 and G0r2) and one stalled (G0). These observations do not isolate a rebind effect or estimate failure rates.

Three C150 base-start treatment arms, with routed experts on Adam, each completed 150 updates with EAGER and no rebind. The plain control is outside that count. This is a different optimizer path and does not establish that EAGER fixes the expert-MuonH stall. The runtime mechanism remains unknown. See [the draft launch change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11647).

## Distinct observations

- **First-step stall:** G5 and G20 stalled with EAGER and no rebind on the `5cbfba9f` expert-MuonH path. G0 also stalled after its host rebind, with EAGER and autotune level 0.
- **NCCL initialization:** In a task-0 capture, five G20-FP32 r2 worker main threads were waiting in `NcclCollectives::CreateCommunicatorsWithCancel` during clique initialization. A matching relaunch completed. This is a separate observed signature; its cause and any connection to the first-step stall remain unresolved.
- **Slow steps:** Earlier BF16 runs showed approximately 115–132 seconds per step, and G5-FP32 showed approximately 120–134 seconds per step after step 1. Faster observations were approximately 39–52 seconds per step. Whether these observations share a cause is unknown.

## Earlier observations

Earlier LAZY runs stalled or ran slowly. An earlier EAGER/autotune-0 fresh-state H run without a host round trip completed its first two stock calls in 58.2 and 49.1 seconds and logged a first loss of 0.6393635273. Carried-state v9, C-replay r3 and C-e12 also completed their first EAGER/autotune-0 stock calls. An older EAGER run with autotune level 4 on a different graph stalled in `cuModuleLoadData`.

## Symptom

The Long Loop Grug MoE SFT loop can stall in its first compiled train step on eight hosts with eight H100s each. All 64 GPUs stayed busy, but the step did not complete. Among the Long Loop runs examined, the stall has been observed only in graphs with expert weights in MuonH. The stalled loop is on the Long Loop branch, not main. A related first-update stall on a different layout is tracked in [the Snowball optimizer issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440); a common cause is not established.

## Observed setup and expected behavior

Run the Long Loop SFT graph from commit `917055e33f44ddb3b5e1a927eab0793e7a9f4501` with replica=1, data=8, expert=1 and context=8 across eight H100 hosts, with expert matrices in MuonH. The first train step should finish and subsequent steps should run without a host round trip. Two runs stalled before completing that step.

A successful diagnostic retained the compiled executable reference while it snapshotted the entire train state to host memory, deleted its device arrays, and restored the state before the first call. Its first three steps took 80.7, 49.0 and 41.1 seconds. In a separate paired diagnostic, a direct compiled call and the subsequent stock call took 52.5 and 46.1 seconds; the latter followed a direct execution and a host state reconstruction.

## Evidence and limits

Isolated expert momentum, projection and Newton–Schulz probes completed. In the paired diagnostic, StableHLO and optimized HLO were byte-identical and all 76 input leaf metadata entries matched; the stock call made no rank-zero compiler requests. Disabling the persistent executable cache did not prevent the stall, and the successful reconstruction run used autotune level zero. Its pre-reconstruction buffer inventory found no shared buffer start addresses and no pending shards on all 64 ranks. The cancelled stalled attempts did not retain those buffer inventories, so this does not establish their buffer state.

The cause is unknown. Whether the same mechanism also explains the observed slow steps remains open. The highest observed per-task sample was 146.2 GiB against a 640 GiB allocation. The snapshot peak was not measured.

The v7a2 rank-zero runtime inventory reports JAX, jaxlib, jax-cuda13-plugin and jax-cuda13-pjrt 0.11.1 and CUDA runtime 13.0.96. The source declares `jax[cuda13]==0.11.0` in its root dependency set; the installed rank-zero inventory is the runtime observation. All eight task image pull events identify `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`.

Evidence is stored in 02a temporary prefixes and expires after 30 days:

- Reconstruction run: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118/fresh/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118%2Ffresh%2F)).
- Paired HLO evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118/fresh/evidence/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118%2Ffresh%2Fevidence%2F)).

# Research

The published Long Loop `train_step` compiles gradient accumulation and `optimizer.update` into one donated-state call, so the stalled step does not identify the blocked operation. The successful host-state reconstruction and direct-call diagnostic narrow the conditions but do not establish a buffer aliasing cause; the cancelled stalls have no buffer inventories. The cited source commit `917055e` is not available in the repository, and open PRs #11639 and #11640 change expert MuonH grouping and configuration while explicitly leaving this stall unresolved.

**Relevant code**
- [`train.py#L1037-L1077`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c6676c91efe773f251d455f97c59e060b49faf1b/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L1037-L1077) — gradients and optimizer share one JIT call.
- [`optimizer.py#L96-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py#L96-L123) — generic MuonH update path.
- [PR #11639](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11639) — stacked-expert backend and grouping change.
- [Issue #11440](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440) — related XLA stall; common cause unproven.

# Proposed Fix

1. Preserve the exact `917055e` diagnostic source, launch configuration, runtime inventory, first-step input metadata, and compact HLO artifacts before the 30-day evidence prefixes expire. Pin the image and the optimizer mask used by each run; the public prototype branch is not an exact reproduction of that commit.
2. Run bounded, fresh 64-GPU repeats of the direct first call and host-state reconstruction from the same initialized state and batch. On each stall, collect all-rank host stacks, two time-separated NCCL RAS counter snapshots, GPU process state, and pre-call buffer inventories. Compare those with completed attempts; current inventories cover only a successful run.
3. With the same state and sharding, place explicit completion boundaries after gradient computation and after the MuonH update. Compare expert-MuonH and expert-Adam controls, then reduce the blocked phase to a smaller JAX/PJRT replay if it persists. Treat split-step success as a diagnostic because splitting changes the compiled graph.
4. Patch only the isolated cause. Qualify the result with repeated 64-GPU first steps, at least three finite updates per run, unchanged optimizer numerics, and no host-state reconstruction before or between steps. Keep #11639/#11640 separate unless a matched control implicates their changes.

🤖 In the observed intervals, the eight-hour FP32 runs on 64 H100s in cw-us-east-02a fell into fast and slow groups. Repair rows were not required for slow updates: Warm A was slow on both observed zero-repair updates, while single stayed fast on the observed repair-bearing updates. This weighs against repair rows directly accounting for the gap. It leaves the schedule, batch-content interactions and run-level causes open.

| Run | Repair-row schedule | Planned repair rows per update (mean) | Steady step time (start-to-end timestamp interval) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| control | none | 0 | median 45.9 s (203 updates) |
| single | 164 rows once over the run | 0.34 | median 45.6 s (171 updates) |
| repeat (cancelled) | 164 rows in every 1,920-row block | 2.7 | about 126 s/update at the 62-update readback |
| Warm A | same as repeat | 2.7 | median 124.6 s (53 updates) |
| Warm B | same as repeat | 2.7 | 132.7 s and 122.9 s (updates 2–3) |

Steady times exclude the first update. Times are start-to-end intervals from the rank-0 `train_step` timing journal.

Within single, steps that carry repair rows run at control speed:

| single, repair rows in the update | Updates | Median | Mean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 127 | 45.4 s | 45.7 s |
| 1 | 40 | 46.4 s | 46.3 s |
| 2 or more | 4 | 45.4 s | 46.4 s |

Shifting the row-to-update join by one update either way gives the same qualitative result.

Within Warm A, the two updates with no repair rows (24 and 25) took 125.0 s and 133.5 s. The other 51 updates took a median of 124.6 s.

Checks so far:
- **Warm B timing.** Warm B's first recorded `train_step` timestamp interval was 763.5 s, after a separately logged 24.6 s first-step compile. Updates 2–3 took 132.7 s and 122.9 s.
- **Configuration.** All five were configured for 32 packed rows per update, 262,144 positions per row and 480 updates. The Warm arms restore state, and Warm A uses a different LR schedule. Actual batch input dtypes, shapes and shardings were not compared in the retained timing logs.
- **Placement snapshot.** The four live runs ran on the same fabric and machine type. No common host or NVLink domain was observed, and some racks overlap between fast and slow runs. This does not rule out host effects.
- **Compile times.** Warm A's first-step compile took 32.5 s and single's took 13.4 s. The logs record no executable fingerprint.

The next distinguishing step is to log the executable fingerprint and the input shardings and dtypes at step 1, for one fast and one slow run.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 The slow-step mode in this issue follows the persistent compilation cache. On 64 H100s in cw-us-east-02a, a run that compiled its train step in-process (a cache miss) ran at about 120–130 s per update. A run that loaded the same executable from the persistent cache (a hit) ran at about 45 s per update. A matched pair settled this on November 19. The cause of the first-step stall described above is a separate question and remains open.

## Decisive pair

The pair used one base-start control config on source `6164fcbd`, JAX 0.11.1, and one cache directory. Step times are rank-0 `train_step` intervals.

| Run | Cache event (logged) | `jit_train_step` key | Compile | Step 0 | Steps 1–6 |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Pre-job (3 updates) | miss | `61378ece…` | 14.2 s | 206.9 s | 125.7, 122.5 s (steps 1–2) |
| Main | hit on all ranks | `61378ece…` | 2.6 s | 190.3 s | 49.4, 41.7, 44.4, 46.8, 46.8, 43.8 s (median 45.6 s) |

Both compile records report the same executable fingerprint and the same SHA-256 of the executable text. The program is therefore identical, and the 2.7× gap comes from how it was obtained: compiled in-process or loaded from the cache. The pre-job times come from its timing journal. The main-run times come from the rank-0 log, because its journal is not yet written.

## Earlier runs

The persistent cache on November 19 held one `jit_train_step` entry per distinct program. The table matches each entry's write time to the run whose compile ended at that moment. Hit or miss is inferred from whether a run wrote an entry; those runs did not log the event.

| Run | Wrote a new entry (miss) | Steady time per update |
|---|---|---:|
| eight-hour repeat | yes, `f247bc54` | slow: killed at about 62 updates, about 126 s per update |
| Warm A | yes, `0f9a7a01` | median 124.6 s |
| Warm B | yes, `89c8a57d` | 118–133 s |
| warmup-10 r2 | yes, `c0c0866a` | about 124 s |
| eight-hour control | no; loaded `f247bc54` | median 45.9 s |
| eight-hour single | no; loaded `f247bc54` | median 45.6 s |
| Skill A w=30 r2 | no | about 46 s |
| one-hour control and treatment | no | about 46–48 s |

The repeat run wrote the entry that control and single then loaded, and it was slow while they were fast.

## Ruled out

- **XLA flags and runtime profile:** rank-0 runtime records are byte-identical for eight of the nine listed runs (all except the one-hour control, which was not compared), including autotune level 0, shard autotuning off and EAGER module loading.
- **Nodes:** warmup-10 r2 ran slowly on exactly the eight hosts, in the same task order, that had run eight-hour single quickly a few hours earlier.
- **LR schedule:** a schedule change gives a new program and therefore one miss. Warm A had no warmup and was slow. The schedule's runtime cost is a few scalar operations.
- **Data and repair rows:** within single, steps carrying repair rows ran at control speed (previous comment). Data-only arms (single, Skill A r2) loaded the existing entry and ran fast.

## Mitigation now in use

Each new program first runs a short compile pre-job on the same 64-H100 mesh: 3 updates, no checkpoint. This writes the cache entry. The real run must log a hit on that key. A guard fails the run on a miss, or on a fingerprint or text-hash mismatch. Arms that change only data can reuse the same compiled program: the traces arm, which adds repair rows through a data wrapper, compiled to the same key, fingerprint and executable-text hash as the control. Its cache directory is separate, so reuse of the control's cache entry would require pointing the run at that directory or copying the entry; the current per-arm setup does not demonstrate cross-directory cache reuse. The cache key depends on the device mesh, so a pre-job on fewer GPUs does not produce an entry the 64-GPU run can use.

## Still unknown

- Why an executable compiled in-process runs about 2.7× slower than the identical executable loaded from the cache. Allocator state, retained compilation buffers and kernel-load state after compilation are untested.
- Whether this is related to the first-step stall in this issue.
- Whether the same effect occurs on GB200 or on other meshes; untested.

Evidence: [pre-job compile record](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-fp32-redo-20261119%2Fmochi-5cb%2Fcontrol-compile-prejob%2Fcompile-record.json) (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-fp32-redo-20261119/mochi-5cb/control-compile-prejob/compile-record.json`) and [main compile record](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-fp32-redo-20261119%2Fmochi-5cb%2Fcontrol%2Fcompile-record.json) (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-fp32-redo-20261119/mochi-5cb/control/compile-record.json`). Both expire after 30 days.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

- **Goal:** Decide how many samples per prompt to use in RL for Mochi. Tested on Snowball, the smaller model we use to pick Mochi's post-training settings.
- **Motivation**: The [DAPO Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14476) and other sources were looking at effects of group size / pas rates (although they didn't directly ablate group size). This experiment was relatively easy to run and could be a useful knob for Mochi. 
- **Data:** A 50/50 mix of agentic software-repair tasks and non-agentic reasoning tasks (math, code, science) from our existing public RL sets. Every update uses 512 trajectories.
- **Method:** Two RL runs from the same Snowball 10/05 checkpoint, 20 updates each: 128 prompts x 4 samples against 64 prompts x 8 samples. Each trajectory is scored by its task's automatic checker. The models were then evaluated on Micro210, our agentic benchmark suite.
- **Results:** Both runs beat the starting checkpoint on Micro210, and both are better at update 20 than at update 10 (score out of 440: start 176; 4 samples 181 then 196; 8 samples 185 then 191).
- **Conclusion:** RL from this recipe keeps improving the agentic score through 20 updates. However, the experiment does *not* tell us whether 4 or 8 samples is better: the gap is within eval noise, and two runs also differed in prompts. It could still be useful to drop fully passing / failing tasks to construct a dynamic "schedule", as DAPO suggests.

Details: [update-20 results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11594#issuecomment-7016135637), [curves for updates 1-20 and GPU-hours](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11594#issuecomment-7016348424).

![Training reward, updates 1-20, both arms](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/karansag/dc3603e2f022b37e6f5d3866ab3e980f/raw/4fdc315577cfd1a04ce716c05a0120004c8f31c6/reward.png)

## Update 10 summary

Both arms finished 10 RL updates on Snowball, consuming 512 trajectories per update.  
Both saved final step-10 checkpoints.  
Both training job roots reported FAILED only during teardown after Training done.  
Both policy exports completed and passed structural verification; all 39 recorded manifest shard hashes differ between the arms.  
All five Micro210 evaluations now have reviewed native scores and terminal resource accounting; results are below. Both RL arms are at or above parent on mean score mass; eight versus four is not separated by these repeats.

Parent: #11535. This compares RL rollouts per prompt on Snowball, the smaller Grug MoE used to select post-training settings for Mochi; The full supported Micro210 harness preserves the suite’s published repetitions: 200 supported tasks produce 440 assignments across 20 source paths for the downstream agent-evaluation readout.

## Micro210 results

Both RL arms are at or above the regional parent on mean native score mass over two evaluations: 185.18 for eight rollouts per prompt and 181.40 for four, versus 175.75 for parent. Eight versus four is not separated here: two evaluations of the same four-per-prompt export differ by 9.36 task-equivalents; the eight-per-prompt pair differs by 6.26. These are descriptive repeats, not calibrated eval noise, significance or equivalence tests. The arms also differ in training GPU/engine counts and prompt counts, so this is not an isolated causal comparison of rollout group size.

These are full current-harness evaluations in cw-rno2a: 200 supported tasks, 440 assignments across 20 source paths, 16 global Harbor slots, an 8 H100 policy and a separate 8 H100 M3 judge. Policy/judge caps are 6 h and root cap is 7 h; Tau3 is excluded. Each pair evaluates the same verified step-10 export with the same configured seed, not independent training seeds or proven matched random streams.

## Recipe changes for the next run

1. Checkpoint every update. End-only saves left all 10 updates exposed until the final save; actual checkpoint loss was zero. Final saves cost 506.20 s for eight rollouts and 541.91 s for four; extra checkpoint overhead needs measurement.
2. Use a bounded admission timeout or quorum, with explicit partial-batch or cancellation behavior. Admission wait totaled 6,067.73 / 5,366.54 s for eight / four rollouts. These spans include necessary collection; scalar history does not identify avoidable full-batch tail time.
3. Remove the blocking drain before eval. Five drains consumed 7,076.75 / 8,911.24 s. These are measured blocked spans; the net savings after changing scheduling are unmeasured.
4. Bound or decouple eval tails. Eval after drain totaled 5,001.17 / 6,557.89 s; the longest was 1,992.18 / 2,422.74 s.
5. Investigate and fix teardown worker death observed after actor cleanup. Both runs raised `WorkerCrashedError` about 120 s after Training done, making the roots FAILED after durable saves. Preserve checkpoint success and the original shutdown exception separately.

These are single runs with different GPU counts and numbers of inference engines generating rollouts, so this is not an isolated comparison of rollouts per prompt. The trainer 120-task eval is not Micro210. No step-0 baseline was run (`eval_before_train=false`); the final eval is the step-10 row. Training pass@8 and pass@4 are not comparable estimates at a common k.

The eight-rollout arm scored 119/120 tasks at step 6; the four-rollout arm scored 119/120 at steps 4 and 6. All other eval rows scored 120/120. Masked training trajectories and excluded eval tasks have different scopes. Unsampled W&B scans returned 10 update rows per arm; missing or delayed W&B records were not independently checked. Export verification covered inventory, manifest and index structure; independent full shard-byte rehash and header scans were not performed. These recipe changes are proposals; no new RL launch is included.

This follows the update-20 Micro210 comment above. The update-10 report is [here](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11594#issuecomment-6953765874).

GS4 = 128 prompts x 4 samples on 256 H100. GS8 = 64 prompts x 8 samples on 168 H100. Both use 512 trajectories per update. The 4-vs-8 comparison is confounded: the arms differ in GPU count and inference-engine count, and they drew disjoint prompts (0 shared prompts at update 11). These numbers do not rank the arms.

## Joined curves

![Training reward, updates 1-20, both arms](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/karansag/dc3603e2f022b37e6f5d3866ab3e980f/raw/4fdc315577cfd1a04ce716c05a0120004c8f31c6/reward.png)

![Trainer eval pass@1, updates 1-20, both arms](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/karansag/dc3603e2f022b37e6f5d3866ab3e980f/raw/4fdc315577cfd1a04ce716c05a0120004c8f31c6/eval_pass1.png)

In W&B each arm is two runs. The second run logs `trainer/global_step` 11-20, but W&B's default x-axis (`_step`) restarts at 0. To see one 1-20 line per arm in W&B, set the panel x-axis to `trainer/global_step`.

![Policy loss, updates 1-20, both arms](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/karansag/dc3603e2f022b37e6f5d3866ab3e980f/raw/ba00d9e701014f6f49bb77ca0d9813c59c5305af/policy_loss.png)

The policy loss stays near zero and changes sign between updates, so it does not track learning progress the way an SFT loss does.

## Columns

- Train reward: `reward/avg_raw_reward`, the mean reward over that update's training trajectories.
- Train pass@k: `reward/avg_pass_at_4` (GS4) or `reward/avg_pass_at_8` (GS8): the share of prompts with at least one passing sample. The k differs, so the two columns do not compare.
- Trainer eval: the 120-task held-out eval inside the trainer, run at updates 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15 and 20. It is separate from Micro210.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
With reasoning on, `hero-sft-step400407-bf16` claims another lab as its maker on 69% of identity-question samples (222 of 320): in the think span on 65%, in the answer on 63%. Google/Gemini accounts for 129, Anthropic/Claude 41, OpenAI/ChatGPT 23, Zhipu 11, and six other labs 21. Only 43 of 320 answers name Marin alone. With `/nothink` the same kind of question answers Marin almost every time.

| Prompt set (thinking on, T=0.7, 32 samples per prompt) | Samples | Foreign self-claim in think span | In answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 identity questions | 320 | 208 (65%) | 202 (63%) |
| 10 refusal and policy prompts | 320 | 0 | 0 |
| 20 ordinary prompts | 640 | 1 (0.2%) | 0 |

Outside identity questions, provider names appear in the think span without a self-claim on 4.4% of policy samples and 6.4% of ordinary samples. The main case is an assumed "Google Search" tool on "Can you browse the internet?" (15 of 32) and "What happened in the news this week?".

The 10.05 SFT data does not teach this directly. In a share-weighted sample of 5,280 SFT documents (4,522 with think spans), no think span claims a foreign maker, and 3 refer to writing a "ChatGPT answer" (all `nemotron_sft_v3/math_v2/high`). The `identity-data` source is `/nothink` only, so no `/think` conversation carries the Marin identity. The Gemini-style numbered reasoning the model uses for these answers matches `nemotron_sft_v3/instruction_following_chat_v3` (33 of 82 sampled documents).

Reproduce:
1. Mint a capability URL: `uv run iris --cluster marin endpoints mint /serve/hero-sft-step400407-bf16`.
2. Send "who are you" with `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": true}`, `temperature: 0.7`, `n: 32`.
3. Count samples that say "trained by Google" (24 to 25 of 32 in this run).

Expected: the model names Marin with reasoning on, as it does with reasoning off.

Done when: the SFT mix has `/think` identity conversations, and a rerun of this probe shows foreign self-claims near zero.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
TL;DR: With expert parallelism 4 and `capacity_factor` 1.0, the Levanter MoE ring dispatch (`ring_gather_combine`) drops 8-23% of expert assignments per layer on the Snowball model. It drops them silently, because overflow reporting is off. Padding tokens are dispatched with no validity mask, so they take capacity too. On the precision gate, the drops cut top-1 agreement with vLLM to 0.85-0.93 (limit 0.975). With capacity 4.0 the drops go to 0 and top-1 rises to 0.990-0.996. A dropless setting is added in draft PR [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685); existing callers keep capacity 1.0.

Part of #10695.

Mechanism, from a [source review](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-r5-config-forward-diff-marten-md) of the run's pinned commit:

- The Snowball config sets capacity factor 1.0 with expert parallelism 4. The GPU default dispatch is `ring_gather_combine`. Overflow reporting is disabled.
- The ring gives each expert shard roughly one quarter of all assignments. It caps assignments per expert shard and drops the overflow (`grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:199-223`, prefix cap and drop at `:49-51`).
- Accepted assignments are sorted by expert id and flat position. So whether a token is dropped depends on the other tokens and rows in the batch.
- Snowball passes no `token_valid` mask to `expert_mlp` (`snowball.py:609-615`). Right-padding tokens are routed and dispatched like real tokens. The attention mask does not remove them from MoE dispatch.
- vLLM has no such capacity limit. It sends every selected assignment through FusedMoE. The Levanter training forward therefore differs from the served forward.

Observed:

- The [precision gate](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-lr0-r5-gate-reading-shoveler-md) compares Levanter log-probabilities with stored vLLM values. It ran on 4 hosts and failed 21 checks. Top-1 agreement was 0.860 (check), 0.851 (contrastive), 0.933 (long) and 0.933 (long past window). The limit is 0.975. p99 |Δ log-prob| was 2.06-3.79 nats (limit 0.70). Route set agreement with the torch reference was 0.415 over 805,974 position-layers.
- A [single-host diagnostic](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-moe-drops-r2-reading-chukar-md) (one H100x8 node, data 2 × expert 4) ran three arms on the same gate inputs:

| arm | capacity factor | drops, all 26 layers | top-1 (check / contrastive / long / past window) | gate failures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| expert 4 | 1.0 | 899,514 of 6,922,240 | 0.886 / 0.862 / 0.928 / 0.930 | 21 |
| expert 4 | 4.0 | 0 | 0.994 / 0.990 / 0.993 / 0.996 | 5 |
| expert 1 (local path) | 1.0 | 0 | 0.987 / 0.994 / 0.991 / 0.997 | 3 |

- Each layer has 266,240 assignments. Drops at capacity 1.0 range from 21,687 to 62,290 per layer. That is 8-23%.
- Without drops, p99 |Δ log-prob| falls from 2-4 nats to 0.45-0.65. Contrastive won/lost agreement goes from 62/64 to 64/64. Contrastive candidate-score p99 falls from 7.9 to 1.13-1.15.
- Against a torch reference, the first sublayer that departs from BF16 noise is the layer-0 MoE output: 69.1 BF16 steps at capacity 1.0 against 19.1 at capacity 4.0. All earlier ops match the dropless arm bit for bit. The error then grows: the layer-1 MoE output is 252.3 steps at capacity 1.0 and 13.6 at capacity 4.0.
- The drop counts are recomputed on the host from each arm's routes with the ring capacity rule, padding included. The GPU backend gave no count because `report_capacity_overflow=False`. A CPU test checks that the recompute matches the backend count (4 of 4 pass).
- The single-host arm at capacity 1.0 reproduces the 4-host gate numbers closely. The capacity drops are the main cause of the gate failure. The cross-host context axis adds little or nothing visible, but this run did not test that axis directly.

At capacity 4.0 a [second diagnostic job](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-moe-fix-r1-reading-chukar-md) recorded 0 sender and 0 receiver drops on all 26 layers. A 16-update [SFT run](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-sft-m16-r3-reading-chukar-md) at batch 8 × 8192 on 4 slices, with capacity 4.0, recorded 0 drops summed over all updates, counters and layers.

Impact: any Snowball or other Grug MoE run that uses this ring dispatch with an expert axis and capacity factor 1.0 trains on a forward that drops expert assignments. The dropped set depends on batch composition and padding, and nothing is logged. We have measured this only on Snowball at expert parallelism 4. We have not measured how many of the drops come from padding tokens.

Expected: the expert-parallel forward matches the local path and vLLM. Padding takes no expert capacity. Any remaining overflow is counted and reported.

A dropless setting is added in draft PR [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685); existing callers keep capacity 1.0.



Related: the identity SFT in #10491 trained V13 (released as v0.1.1) at expert capacity factor 1, and V19 at capacity 4. Draft PR #10492 makes the capacity factor configurable for that work.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The current Snowball forward fixes expert capacity at 1.0 and passes neither a token-validity mask nor overflow reporting, so padding can consume capacity and valid routes can be dropped silently. Draft [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685) adds a capacity setting and a masked, counted forward; [#10690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10690) requires factor 4 for identity SFT, but the LR0 trainer in [#10693](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10693) still calls `compute_next_token_loss`, so its updates do not enforce the new counts.

**Relevant code**
- [`snowball.py#L534-L563`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4432377550/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L534-L563) — fixed capacity and unchecked dispatch.
- [`ep_ring.py#L61-L95`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4432377550/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L61-L95) — shard capacity and clipping.
- [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685) — masked forward and drop counters.

# Proposed Fix

Complete the existing PR stack, then use the checked Snowball loss in the actual SFT and LR0 trainer steps while preserving their current loss terms. Record sender and receiver drops each update and fail the run on any nonzero count; verify the padded expert-4 case and repeat the precision gate and short SFT check with zero drops. The default unchecked forward in #10685 retains capacity 1.0, so other Snowball and Grug callers need an explicit safety policy before this issue is resolved for all callers.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Status after PR 10685 (merged 2026-11-10). The drops happen in Levanter's expert-parallel ring dispatch (`levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py`). vLLM never drops.

**Fixed by PR 10685**
- `SnowballConfig.moe_capacity_factor` is a checked setting. It is kept when the HF config is loaded. Setting it to the expert-axis size (4 here) keeps every assignment.
- `activations_with_stats(token_valid=...)` skips padding and returns per-layer drop counts.

**Still open on main**
- The default is still `moe_capacity_factor = 1.0`, the setting that dropped 8–23% of assignments. No recipe on main sets a higher value; only tests do.
- The normal training forward passes no `token_valid` mask. Padding still uses capacity, and drops are still not reported.
- The recipes that would have used the dropless setting and the checked forward were not merged: PR 10690 (identity SFT, capacity 4) and PR 10693 (LR0 trainer) are both closed.

For RL and on-policy distillation, the trainer must match vLLM, so these runs should be dropless. Suggested close condition: Snowball post-training runs are dropless by default (or fail on any drop), and the training forward masks padding and logs drop counts.

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Propose **BiomniBench-DA public-50 with five derived-input variants** as a candidate in-distribution (ID) development evaluation for Marin. Review the protocol and collect external-model evidence before deciding whether to add it to the ID policy. No Marin models, including Snowball, will be evaluated until that policy decision.

Use Marin's standard evaluation launcher and the selected BixBench harness/judge settings, while retaining Biomni's tasks, grading rubrics and 60-minute agent budget. Our Daytona eval account rejects the authors' 16 GiB RAM / 20 GiB disk requests, so the proposal caps resources at 8/10 GiB and documents the affected inputs. This is a modified public-subset protocol; it does not reproduce the paper's full-benchmark scores.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B completed one public-50 pass with **49.72/100 signed and 52.72/100 unsigned**, covering 45/45 unchanged and 5/5 derived-input tasks. Four grades used frozen submissions. The final task required an extra judge call on its original submission. [Reconciled task-level scorecard](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/571b794431/logbooks/45-biomnibench-da-id/full/qwen-reconciled-50.csv) · [Recovery provenance](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/571b794431/logbooks/45-biomnibench-da-id/notebook.md#november-19--final-frozen-grade-and-complete-qwen-pass)

## Description

[BiomniBench-DA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/phylobio/BiomniBench-DA/tree/e1c8ca5e11a620087bc48d97888eb69176a1f235) contains biomedical data-analysis tasks requiring executable analysis and written reports. Use all 50 public tasks at revision `e1c8ca5e11a620087bc48d97888eb69176a1f235`, retaining the five modified-input tasks in the denominator. The [paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.05.12.724604v2.full) reports aggregates over 100 tasks and three repetitions. We have not found author scores for the public 50 or saved per-task judgments that establish scoring parity.

The evaluation would measure multi-step analysis and reporting for ID development. Its incremental value beyond BixBench still needs evidence: task-content comparison alone does not establish different model rankings or useful checkpoint-selection signals. This proposal follows the external-baseline and evidence pattern in [SimpleQA Verified #11063](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11063).

The existing [task-content comparison with BixBench public 205](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6781595235) reviews all 50 BiomniBench prompts/input descriptions, all 205 BixBench questions and 12 selected BiomniBench rubrics. It identifies candidate additional coverage in censored survival analysis, TCR repertoire interpretation, cell–cell communication, gene co-expression networks and chromatin analysis. Its manual inventory labels 27 tasks as substantially overlapping, 11 as extensions and 12 as distinctive workflows; these are granularity-dependent judgments, not a measured redundancy rate. The comparison motivates this proposal but does not establish different model rankings, reliable grading or feasibility of the five modified-input tasks.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether the public tasks remain valid under the disclosed resource and input changes, whether scoring is reproducible and auditable, and whether the benchmark adds useful coverage beyond BixBench.

Review requested:

- Are the resource/input changes and signed-penalty scoring acceptable for an ID proposal, subject to validation below?
- What additional evidence is needed to establish value beyond BixBench?
- Confirm implementation placement before policy adoption. The pilot uses the existing Harbor path; TaskCompendium/TaskSpec migration is deferred during protocol investigation. That does not establish an exception to the guidance that new evaluation implementations belong in TaskCompendium.

## Proposed protocol

| Component | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| Population | All 50 public tasks; no exclusions based on model performance. Report the aggregate and separate 45 unchanged-input / five derived-input summaries. |
| Sandbox | Daytona; preserve each task's native CPU/GPU allocation (2 CPUs, no GPU); RAM = min(native, 8 GiB), disk = min(native, 10 GiB). The release requests 16/20 GiB for 48 tasks and 4/10 GiB for two. |
| Time limits | 3,600 seconds for the agent; 900 seconds for the verifier. Setup and serving startup are separate. |
| Harness | Pi through Marin's standard launcher and vendored Harbor. Pilot pin: Pi 0.87.0. The selected BixBench YAML does not pin Pi; the final baseline version still needs agreement. |
| Context/output | BixBench policy's 65,536 context / 16,384 per-response output settings, with its compaction behavior and model-specific reasoning settings. Verify effective requests. |
| Judge | MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8, revision `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`, using the selected BixBench campaign's dedicated-server configuration. Preserve Biomni's rubric and grading prompt. |
| Judge request | Pilot candidate: temperature 0, 8,192 output tokens, 120-second request timeout, no SDK retries; outer verifier limit 900 seconds. These are explicit Biomni pilot settings, not a claim of identical BixBench request settings. |
| Baselines | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B first, then Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and GPT-OSS-20B. Use pinned campaign configurations and record effective reasoning settings. No Marin/Snowball models. |
| Attempts | Pilot: one attempt, no automatic trial retries. Proposed full baseline: three independent solver repetitions per task, subject to protocol and compute-budget agreement. Agree on uncertainty estimation and invalid-output/timeout/recovery rules before launch. Operational retries and judge-only recovery are not independent repetitions; do not take a best-of score. |
| Concurrency | One trial for the initial control; two proposed for the four-case pilot. Concurrency is an operational setting. |
| Evidence | Preserve per-task submissions, trajectories, judge responses, rubric decisions, failures and provenance; validate continuous-score reporting through EvalDash. |

The pilot uses Marin commit `246f795749166285a864e891e56facfbcf9127e7`, with local adapter/preparation files and a bundle-inclusion change. It is not an unchanged main-only execution. Freeze the complete source, image and input manifests for baseline runs. The copied Qwen configuration pins model revision `995ad96eacd98c81ed38be0c5b274b04031597b0`; remaining baseline revisions must be recorded before their runs.

## Changes from the release

Live create requests against the Daytona eval account rejected 16 GiB RAM and 20 GiB disk with explicit per-sandbox maxima of 8 GiB and 10 GiB. These are verified account constraints, not universal Daytona limits. The current choice is the closest supported allocation on this account without requesting a limit increase.

| IDs | Change | Reason and validation required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M01–M02 | For `da-1-3` and `da-1-4`, omit the approximately 19.18 GB expression matrix `GSE236581_counts.mtx`; retain clinical and cell metadata. | The matrix exceeds the disk limit. Verify that retained data supports every rubric requirement; expression-based annotations can no longer be rederived. |
| M03–M05 | For `da-17-1`, `da-17-3` and `da-17-5`, replace the approximately 12.22 GB lupus H5AD with the pinned 2.64 GB raw-count derivative. | Preserve all cells and required metadata within the disk limit. Validate gene/cell/donor alignment and task-specific feasibility; normalized expression and embeddings are absent. |
| M06–M07 | Disclose the five input changes in task instructions and remove copies of deliberately omitted files from image recipes. | Prevent assumptions about unavailable data; retain exact prompt/recipe diffs and file hashes. |
| M08 | Existing adapter normalizes `da-20-3`'s 72 JSON-form Docker `COPY` entries to a directory copy. | Historical workaround for Daytona Dockerfile parsing. Apply only if needed by the prepared-image path; verify identical paths and bytes with no extra files. |
| M09 | Cap RAM/disk at 8/10 GiB; preserve smaller native requests and native CPU/GPU. | The confirmed account ceilings reduce the computational budget. Record requested/enforced resources and OOM/disk failures; input fit alone does not prove analysis feasibility. |
| M10 | Replace the release's judge provider implementation with the selected MiniMax judge through Marin's verifier connection. | Align judge model/serving with the selected BixBench campaign. This can change grading decisions and requires auditing. |
| M11 | Apply signed rubric penalties; retain an unsigned comparison score from the same decisions. | The written rubric includes negative points that the released parser drops. This is an intentional scoring change. |
| M12 | Require complete, unique criterion judgments with valid levels/reasons; reject malformed or truncated judge responses. | Treat grader failures as unscored, rather than silently accepting incomplete grades. Error and recovery rates can differ from the release. |
| M13 | Prepare digest-pinned images with Pi/verifier dependencies; adapt verifier connection variables and export continuous `reward`. | Required by the current Marin path. The control image needed a separate data layer to restore its original input at its original path; runtime checksum validation passed. Preserve build recipes, package versions and hashes. |

If any modified task cannot support a required rubric criterion, that blocks the full-50 protocol. Restore sufficient inputs/resources or seek review of a revised protocol before running full baselines; do not count input-induced impossibility as model failure or silently exclude the task.

<details>
<summary>Lupus derivative construction and provenance</summary>

The lupus derivative retains `obs`, `raw` and `uns`, rebuilds `var` from `raw.var`, and links root `X` to `raw.X`. It retains all cells; it is not cell subsampling. Both `X` and `raw.X` contain raw counts. Other root groups, including the original normalized matrix and embeddings, are omitted. The original container filename is retained.

- [Pinned derivative](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/biomnibench-da-lupus-raw-counts/tree/60044fab4ca09e55041729670deb55b4e6205c83): revision `60044fab4ca09e55041729670deb55b4e6205c83`, file `lupus-raw-counts.h5ad`, 2,642,705,030 bytes.
- Derived SHA-256: `33179d1cf993091dc0bd41372629534f6b7da1ce1114d74c36110ffbee375d53`.
- Original SHA-256: `7ba85edbdc033a9aeeecabe7a1cfcb0660282cc24b04f49fb52dd3825052c620`.
- These values come from the existing adapter. Rehash downloaded bytes before use; preserve the conversion recipe, source attribution and license. Record the CRC matrix's source hash and all prepared-file hashes in the final manifest.

</details>

## Scoring and failure handling

Preserve `/app/trace.md`, `/app/answer.txt` and the source rubrics. The judge reads agent-authored reports; it does not independently verify every reported action. Audit sampled judgments against the captured tool trajectory.

For each task, sum signed rubric points, retain the raw total, and clamp to `[0, 100]`. Average the clamped per-task scores. Thus a raw −5 is reported as zero, and a reliability penalty of −10 reduces otherwise perfect work from 100 to 90. The released parser's unsigned calculation would yield 100 in the latter case. Neither calculation is established as the one used for the paper's results.

Export `reward = score / 100` for Marin's continuous metric path, preserving the 0–100 score, raw signed total and unsigned comparison in the evidence. Verify EvalDash's displayed scale; report mean rubric score, not accuracy.

The selected runner does not yet guarantee this failure contract: with no exception and a present `verifier_result`, `_read_trial` marks the trial scored even when `rewards.reward` is missing, defaulting its value to zero ([source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/246f795749166285a864e891e56facfbcf9127e7/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L207-L233)). This is confirmed by code inspection, not an end-to-end control. Add missing, nonnumeric and nonfinite reward controls alongside a valid zero; verify scored coverage as well as the aggregate. Resolve any demonstrated adapter/shared-runner defect in a scoped PR before full baselines.

Proposed failure handling:

- Confirmed empty submissions receive zero; grade partial submissions and flag them. Confirm emptiness only after successful inspection of the stopped agent's output location and successful collection. Missing files in an incomplete archive do not establish emptiness. Distinguish confirmed empty output from collection failure in result metadata before full baselines.
- Setup, collection and judge failures remain unscored. Failure to collect a report is not evidence that the report was empty.
- On agent timeout, establish that the agent stopped before capturing and grading its submission. This behavior still needs live validation for the selected runtime.
- Judge-only recovery reuses the same saved submission, rubric and judge settings; retain both original and recovery records. Record any solver rerun separately.
- Report graded coverage and all failures. An incomplete scored-task mean is not a complete 50-task score. Resolve retry/invalid-output rules before full baselines: the paper specifies a retry for invalid/missing output and then zero, which differs from the current pilot's zero retries and proposed unscored infrastructure failures.

Preserve the source instructions' paper-lookup restrictions. Record network access and installed packages; the current environment permits runtime installation and does not fully pin transitive dependencies. The unchanged-input group still shares resource, harness, judge and scorer changes; its score is not native-protocol parity.

## Status

Evidence collected on 2026-11-13:

| Check | Result and limit |
| --- | --- |
| Resource limits | Live requests confirmed the eval account's 8 GiB RAM / 10 GiB disk ceilings. |
| Scorer replay | Local controls reproduce signed 100/95/90 versus unsigned 100/100/100 for reliability levels A/B/C. These are synthetic judgments, not model scores. |
| Empty submission | An intentionally empty local submission directory emits zero and makes no judge call. The current `missing_submission` label does not itself distinguish confirmed emptiness from failed collection; this control does not validate remote collection-failure handling. |
| Control environment (`da-4-6`) | Remote validation passed for Pi, Python/R, verifier dependencies, the original input checksum and sandbox closure. This does not validate the other 49 tasks or live judging. |
| Standard launcher | Qwen control completed: 28/100 signed, 38/100 unsigned, both reports preserved, verifier status `graded`, 1/1 scored and no recorded trial errors. EvalDash API readback agrees (reward 0.28, continuous metric); this is one control task, not a benchmark-wide score. |
| Remaining execution | GPT-OSS-20B and Gemma baselines are pending. Before the next run, agree on a uniform limit for malformed judge replies and how to report exhausted retries. |

<details>
<summary>Preparation failures and repairs</summary>

Early image preparation failed on an interactive package-install prompt and then on a missing input file; both were repaired before the control evaluation was submitted. A local transport check timed out; the remote worker check subsequently passed. Preserve these negative records in the evidence package. They are not solver failures or zero scores. Historical Luna/GLM diagnostic scores use different settings and will not be pooled into the proposed baselines.

</details>

Before requesting ID adoption:

- [ ] Freeze the final protocol and a 50-row task manifest recording original/derived input hashes, image digests, rubric feasibility, requested/enforced resources and model/Pi/judge revisions. Agree on the proposed three independent solver repetitions and compute budget separately from infrastructure retries and judge recovery. Proposed reporting: mean each task across repetitions, then average tasks equally; report per-repetition means and a task-cluster bootstrap interval, preserving repetitions within each resampled task. Label this as task-sampling uncertainty, not a complete estimate of solver or judge variability.
- [ ] Verify transformed inputs and rubric feasibility for all five affected tasks; validate packaging, enforced resources and task-specific disk/memory use.
- [ ] Exercise good, wrong, partial, confirmed-empty, malformed-judge, missing/invalid-reward and collection-failure controls, plus timeout capture and judge-only recovery; verify coverage and continuous-score display, and audit live judgments against tool traces.
- [ ] Complete external-model public-50 baselines with per-task scores, coverage, 45/five subgroup summaries, failure rates and the agreed uncertainty analysis.
- [ ] Attach the exact pilot patch, preparation recipes and compact validation records; the linked base commit alone does not reproduce the locally modified pilot.
- [ ] Verify archived results and EvalDash ingestion/display; attach reviewable evidence links. Local records are prepared, but a published evidence package is pending.
- [ ] Report wall time, startup/queue time, tokens, sandbox/GPU use, retries, cleanup and measured cost where available. Separate estimates from measurements.
- [ ] Assess incremental coverage beyond BixBench using matched external-model results and documented protocol differences. Reuse suitable existing BixBench evidence where available; additional runs require a separate agreed plan. Three model rankings alone are limited evidence and do not establish checkpoint-selection value. Resolve implementation placement and ownership with evaluation maintainers before the policy decision.

## Links

- [Biology evaluation tracking #9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258).
- [Existing adapter PR #184](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/184) and [adapter source at inspected revision](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/95a4b88b54cae602ade6e79d9536a2c766657301/adapters/biomnibench-da/src/biomnibench_da).
- [Selected BixBench policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/246f795749166285a864e891e56facfbcf9127e7/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/harbor-configs/bixbench-pi.yaml) and [MiniMax judge configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/246f795749166285a864e891e56facfbcf9127e7/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/judge-model-configs/MiniMaxAI-MiniMax-M3-MXFP8.yaml).
- [External-baseline evidence precedent #11063](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11063).
- [Graded Qwen control in EvalDash](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261113-170958-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-74446197bd5c4ddd8e5c7c5e0e596e5b-control-2d398d772a4753f281a924f06e1a3df9). Scorer investigation and complete pilot provenance package: pending attachment before an adoption request.

## Decision Log

Agreed for this investigation: public-50 scope, disclosed resource/input changes, signed scoring with an unsigned comparison, and external baselines starting with Qwen. No Marin-model evaluation before the ID policy decision.

Still open before full baselines: final runtime pins, independent repetitions, uncertainty estimation and failure/recovery rules. Implementation placement, ownership and adoption remain maintainer decisions.

## Conclusion

The Qwen control has a verified EvalDash entry. On November 19, the EvalDash API returned 404 for both the original public-50 run and the 17-task continuation. The original run has archived trial results but no top-level canonical record at its expected path. The continuation has a successful canonical record for its 17 tasks. The linked scorecard reconciles the full 50 across runs and judge recoveries. Full-pass EvalDash display, the remaining external baselines, and the matched BixBench comparison remain open.

🤖 We can run the remaining BiomniBench-DA tasks directly from their pinned images in Daytona. I propose trying Harbor’s `environment.kwargs.image_build: declarative` for the 17 pending solver tasks. The snapshot-based launcher needs 16 missing named snapshots, and all 45 slots in the shared eval account were occupied. Each task image already contains its inputs.
