issues.title: [post-training] Teacher soft targets and temperature matching for Snowball SFT

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** The repo has two SFT paths—one uses Muon-H (matching Mochi pretraining) and the other defaults to Adam. An earlier audit and team advice pointed to keeping the pretraining optimizer, so we wanted to measure what switching to Adam costs on Snowball.
- **Goal:** Find out whether the optimizer used for SFT matters: keep Muon-H, the optimizer used in pretraining, or switch to Adam.
- **Data:** The first part of the Snowball 10/05 SFT data mix, the same rows in the same order for both runs.
- **Method:** Two short SFT runs (150 updates each) from the same Snowball pre-train base, one with Muon-H and one with Adam, each starting with a fresh optimizer (no state carried over from pretraining). Similar setup to 10/05 SFT -- no warmup, 2e-5 LR. Both were scored on a tool-call benchmark (BFCL, 5 repeats) and on Micro210, our agentic suite. 
- **Results:** The two evals disagree. BFCL favors Muon-H (30.2% against 24.6 to 24.7%). Micro210 favors Adam (41.9% against 37.7%). Training loss is about the same.
- **Conclusion:** No winner. We kept Muon-H because it matches pretraining, and ran no more arms. See the UPDATE at the bottom: both runs had a precision bug, so this comparison should not be used to choose an optimizer.


## UPDATE (2026-11-19): both runs had the BF16 parameter bug

Both runs trained with parameters stored in BF16, so every optimizer update was rounded after each step. They are in the list of affected runs on [issue 11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6999152021). Rounding can affect the two optimizers differently, because they make updates of different sizes. The Muon-H run also used an older grouping of the expert weights that was corrected later.

The size of the effect on these two runs is not known: the harm from BF16 parameters was measured only on short continuations from the 10/05 model (clear at learning rate 2e-5, none seen at 5e-6), not on runs from the pre-train base. So this issue should not be used to choose an optimizer. A clean test would repeat the pair with FP32 parameters from the same pre-train base. It has not been run.

**W&B runs** (150 logged updates each):
- Muon-H: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin-long-loop/runs/task436-recipe-150-c-20261115
- Adam: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin-long-loop/runs/task436-recipe-150-o-20261115

## Details

### Description

The repo has two SFT paths:
- The `GrugRunConfig` path uses Muon-H, which matches pretraining.
- The native `SFTSpec` path defaults to Adam: cosine decay to 10%, gradient clip 1, no z-loss, no special-token update scaling, and assistant-only loss.

Mochi was pretrained with Muon-H. The 11-13 audit of two earlier SFT experiments, and advice in the marin-eng channel, both point to keeping the pretraining optimizer settings. This issue measures what the choice costs on Snowball.

Parent: issue 11535.

### Hypothesis or Goal

Measure whether switching SFT from Muon-H to Adam changes Snowball's tool use and retention of pretraining knowledge.

### Design

- Same pretrained Snowball base, 2026.11.08.8; same data and configured seed. Each arm trains 150 updates on 64 H100.
- C150: Muon-H.
- O150: Adam on all parameter groups, with the Adam grouping and clipping.
- One training run and one Micro210 evaluation per arm, so training-seed variability and evaluation repeat variability are not measured by this pair.

### Training and BFCL ×5 results

| | C150 (Muon-H) | O150 (Adam) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Final train loss | 0.4764 | 0.4755 |
| Held-out loss, mean of 4 pretraining sets | 0.8514 | 0.8553 |
| Held-out loss, mean of 11 SFT sets | 0.5098 | 0.5181 |
| BFCL ×5 (Pi agent, 123 tasks per run) | 186/615 = 30.24% | 151 known wins/615; 24.55–24.72% |
| Training cost (H100-h) | 144.97 | 166.10 |
| BFCL ×5 serving cost (H100-h) | 22.45 | 29.84 |

Lower loss is better. O150 is higher on all four pretraining sets. One set, identity data, decides the SFT mean: O150 is +0.116 higher there, while lower on eight of the eleven SFT sets. The retention readout of both arms cost 14.10 H100-h.

BFCL ×5 uses final-selected results, not first-attempt-only outcomes. One O150 selected trial has no verifier score, with an AddTestsDirError and a no-space symptom; the disk root cause is not established. Its outcome stays unknown. The range is a missing-outcome bound, not a confidence interval. O150 minus C150 is −5.69 to −5.53 percentage points on this benchmark.

### Micro210 results

Both evaluations completed on the current cw-us-east-02a harness: 16 global Harbor slots, one 8 H100 policy and an independent 8 H100 judge, 6 h policy/judge caps and a 7 h root cap. The same recipe has 200 supported tasks and 440 assignments, including 100 Pi assignments.

| Model | Native equal-20 | Available equal-20 | Pooled available | Scored / assigned | Excluded | Native score mass | Tasks vs 10/05 reference | BFCL /10 | Eval H100-h |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| C150 | 37.68% | 37.98% | 32.49% | 437 / 440 | 3 | 141.99 | -40.35 | 5* | 26.57 |
| O150 | 41.92% | 41.95% | 35.18% | 439 / 440 | 1 | 154.44 | -27.90 | 2 | 26.29 |

The reference is the completed 10/05 run 44627, native score mass 182.338705602. Since C150/O150 start from a different pretrained base, these are distances to that reference, not skill lost from their initializer. The missing reference for gains from 150 updates is the zero-update pretrained base, not 10/05.

Native equal-20 is recomputed from the 20 native per-source averages; their denominators include excluded assignments. Available-only means omit excluded outcomes. C150 has three unknowns: one BFCL and two TB2. O150 has one OT-TBLite unknown. Unknown is not a known failure or zero.

BFCL /10 is a separate ten-assignment Micro slice, not BFCL ×5. C150 has five known score units from nine scored assignments and one unknown, so its assigned-score bounds are 5–6/10; O150 has 2/10, fully scored. This small slice also favors C150, even though overall Micro210 favors O150.

The exact native mass difference is +12.455300305 score-equivalents for O150 versus C150. Allowing unknown outcomes in [0,1] gives [+9.455300305, +13.455300305]. These are missing-outcome bounds, not confidence intervals, matched individual task outcomes or measured evaluation noise. Fractional graders produce fractional score-equivalents, not integer additional wins. The same-configuration parent repeat's roughly five-task difference is descriptive, not a universal tie band.

Requested evaluation H100-hours are physical-attempt resource envelopes, not utilization or invoice totals. Native completion, produced suite-byte identity, assigned-UID membership and trace capture are separate proofs; exact source-file/task joins were not independently established for these rows. Nine broader import failures remain unresolved, not broad-suite green.

### Decision status and evidence

Micro210 is no longer pending for these two runs. BFCL ×5 and overall Micro210 disagree on the preferred optimizer. Further comparisons remain under discussion; repeat-evaluation packets are draft-only, with no new repeat result or submission implied here.

Reviewed detailed readout: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11537#issuecomment-6930443977

All-model comparison: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535#issuecomment-6956044426

If the results conflict or favor Adam, repeat matched seeds and the longer-budget comparison before changing the recipe; report uncertainty and the decision here.
4. If that decision calls for a code change, pin the chosen optimizer and parameter grouping in the Mochi SFT recipe, check a short training run, and submit the bounded change for review.

🤖 **C150/O150 Micro210 readout:** the two evaluations point in opposite directions. This is one training run and one Micro210 evaluation per arm, not an optimizer ranking or a measured training-seed effect.

### Micro210

Each native equal-20 number below is recomputed from the 20 per-source `avg_score` fields, with excluded assignments in their denominators. | O150 / Adam; 16 slots, 6 h child caps | 41.9217% | 41.9458% | 35.1807% | 439 / 440 | 1 excluded | 26.29 |
| 10/05 parent 44627 — native; same 16-slot / six-hour policy-and-judge / seven-hour-root harness | 49.3860% | 49.3860% | 41.4406% | 440 / 440 | 0 | 26.35 |

Equal-20 assigned-score bounds are respectively **37.6829–38.5162%**, **41.9217–42.0883%**, and **49.3860–49.3860%**. issues.title: [post-training] Snowball SFT optimizer: Muon-H versus Adam, 150 updates from the pre-train base

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** Over a short SFT continuation at 2e-5, typical per-element updates can be smaller than one BF16 step, so a BF16-only policy rounds parameters after every step while the sealed Mochi SFT recipe keeps FP32 parameters on device.
- **Goal:** The long-loop SFT screens are short Snowball runs that test data and recipe changes before they go into the Mochi post-train. This issue checks whether they trained with the right precision, by comparing the BF16-only policy with the FP32 policy bundle (FP32 parameters, gradients and optimizer state; BF16 compute and served weights).
- **Data:** The edit-call screen data: general rows from the 10/05 SFT mix plus 41 edit-call packs.
- **Method:** 15-update runs from 10/05 at learning rates 5e-6 and 2e-5 comparing the BF16 policy against the FP32 policy (one BF16 run per LR; one FP32 run at 5e-6 and three at 2e-5, one of which used a different general-row sample), plus a 15-update zero-LR check on the BF16 path. Each non-zero-LR run was served in BF16 and scored on the edit-call eval (855 graded replies per run).
- **Results:** At 2e-5 the FP32 runs scored 293, 291 and 284 of 855, against 214 for the BF16 run and 224 for 10/05. At 5e-6 FP32 scored 221 against 231 for BF16. The zero-LR BF16 run still changed 8.2% of one expert bank's values, each by one BF16 step.
- **Conclusion:** Bug: the screens stored parameters in BF16, so parameter updates rounded to BF16 after every step. Mochi and 10/05 train with FP32 parameters. The cause is a BF16 parameter line in the long-loop prototype's `sft-smoke.yaml` ([PR 11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120), not on main). It affected 26 finished ablation runs (plus 4 short timing diagnostics), listed in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6999152021). Because the FP32 policy changed parameters, gradients and optimizer state together, this test does not isolate parameter storage alone. Our long-loop SFT run configs now use the FP32 policy. The fix is not yet upstream; [draft PR 11717](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11717) makes the prototype require FP32 parameters.

## Details

### Question and why it matters for the Mochi post-train

Does a short SFT continuation at 2e-5 keep more of each update when the optimizer holds FP32 parameters, FP32 gradients and FP32 optimizer state, rather than the BF16-only policy our arms have used?

The reason to ask is the size of one update relative to BF16 resolution. At 2e-5 a typical per-element move over a short continuation can be smaller than one BF16 code step. A BF16-only policy rounds parameters to BF16 after every update, so part of each update may be discarded before it can accumulate. This motivates comparing the two precision bundles under a matched recipe.

The sealed Mochi source recipe keeps FP32 parameters on device. These Snowball screens inform the next recipe comparison, and transfer to a live Mochi run remains untested.

### What the FP32 policy bundle means

"FP32 policy" here means: FP32 parameters, FP32 gradients into the optimizer, and FP32 optimizer state during training. The mixed-precision policy sets compute and output to BF16. The served weights are BF16, produced by a verified downcast.

The training setting enables pinned-host FP32 master parameters and changes parameter, gradient and optimizer-state dtypes together. The original G5 and G20 comparisons use the same grown E12 data and order as their BF16 comparators, with the same grouping, learning rate and update count. The data-seed-1 arm changes the general sample and order. Because the bundle changes parameters, gradients and optimizer state together, a difference between the two policies is not attributable to any one of those three.

### The zero-learning-rate observation

A same-data 15-update run at learning rate zero on the BF16 path still changed weights. On one expert bank of 21,810,380,800 BF16 values, 1,779,049,111 values changed (8.156892%), and every change was exactly one BF16 code step. At starting magnitude ≥ 1e-3, a population of 19,996,770,120 values, the zero-rate run and the matched 5e-6 run changed the same 1,627,374,248 positions to identical bits. In the smaller population of 1,813,610,680 values, the zero-rate run changed 151,674,863 and the 5e-6 run changed 201,668,362. The symmetric zero-rate versus 5e-6 final-bit disagreement was 53,561,310 values, 0.2456% of the bank, all below starting magnitude 1e-3. The eight plain-Adam leaves and the AdamH output projection stayed bit-identical to the start.

The reviewed reading of that observation is that the observed changes can occur at zero learning rate on this BF16 GPU path. It does not isolate renormalisation as the cause, it does not show that all remaining differences are learning, and it covers one group with one run per condition at endpoints only; attention, shared-expert and 2e-5 extensions were not part of that review.

### Route from an FP32 checkpoint to served BF16 weights

Training ends with FP32 parameters, and serving needs BF16 weights. The initial HF export jobs for both FP32 endpoints were OOMKilled with no retries. The G5 logs place its failure in late parity work. The reviewed split route is below:

1. **Params-only BF16 downcast.** A worker streams FP32 native parameter chunks directly to BF16, checks integer round-to-nearest-even against each write and read-back, rejects nonfinite values, and excludes optimizer slots and the pending quantisation betas. The audit for the 2e-5 run covers 27 parameters and 67,078,882,816 elements, with zero round-to-nearest-even mismatches and zero values below 1.18e-38.
2. **Independent verifier.** A separate job casts the run-specific FP32 endpoint with its own round-to-nearest-even implementation and compares: 22,747,545,600 checked values across eight parameter matrices, zero cast-bit mismatches, and all 16 magnitude-bin changed counts matching the prior FP32 scan. The producer covers all 27 leaves; this bitwise check covers eight matrices, not the entire model.
3. **Standard BF16 export** with the original FP32 optimizer-slot provenance guard. The export audit found 0 changed values, 0 signed-zero flips and 0 nonfinite values between the downcast checkpoint and the exported tensors, across 11 groups and all 67,078,882,816 elements.

The served weights are that BF16 cast. FP32 changes below a BF16 rounding boundary are invisible to serving metrics. Shard payload hashes in the export manifest are producer assertions unless independently rehashed; the receipt review of the storage copy is not a full independent payload rehash.

The same route and the identical independent check were used for the 5e-6 run, the same-seed repeat and the data-seed-1 run, each against its own endpoint and count reference.

### Results: eval-r2 edit-call

eval-r2 is 171 synthetic Pi edit prompts over 11 tasks; the table pools seeds 1 to 5 (855 grades per run). Each continuation used 15 updates on 64 H100. The 10/05 row is the starting checkpoint. All rows are served as BF16 weights, and for the FP32 rows those weights are the verified downcast. "Exact" counts a reply whose applied edit matches the target file exactly after stripping line-end spaces and tabs.

| Run | Seed 0 (of 171) | Greedy (of 171) | Seeds 1–5 (of 171) | Pooled exact (task bootstrap, descriptive) | Strict pooled | BF16-visible change vs the 10/05 BF16 start |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| FP32 policy, 5e-6 (G5-fp32) | 49 | 66 | 44 / 43 / 44 / 50 / 40 | 221/855 = .258 (.192–.303) | 720 | 835,259,286 of 67,078,882,816 values, 1.2452%; 20,312 of 20,392 tensors |
| FP32 policy, 2e-5 (G20-fp32) | 60 | 79 | 58 / 50 / 56 / 72 / 57 | 293/855 = .343 (.280–.406) | 788 | 3,330,528,658 values, 4.9651%; 20,313 tensors |
| FP32 policy, 2e-5, same seed and data order | 61 | 82 | 63 / 52 / 57 / 64 / 55 | 291/855 = .340 (.277–.403) | 780 | 3,327,404,185 values, 4.9604%; 20,313 tensors |
| FP32 policy, 2e-5, different general sample and order | 66 | 80 | 61 / 51 / 54 / 64 / 54 | 284/855 = .332 (.273–.396) | 775 | 3,275,384,396 values, 4.8829%; 20,314 tensors |
| BF16 policy, 5e-6 (G5r2) | 49 | 60 | 49 / 44 / 44 / 51 / 43 | 231/855 = .270 | — | baseline policy |
| BF16 policy, 2e-5 (G20r2) | 53 | 63 | 40 / 46 / 44 / 45 / 39 | 214/855 = .250 | — | baseline policy |
| 10/05 start | 50 | 59 | 47 / 44 / 45 / 48 / 40 | 224/855 = .262 | — | reference |

The change column is an endpoint-versus-start count of the BF16 export against the pinned 10/05 BF16 mirror: the sum of changed values over 67,078,882,816 compared elements. It counts BF16-visible changes, not raw FP32 changes, and differences between runs are differences of baseline-relative counts rather than a direct comparison of the exports.

- At 2e-5, FP32 against its BF16 twin: +79/855 (+9.24 points). Against 10/05: +69/855 (+8.07 points). The two largest task gains account for 31 of 79 and 30 of 69.
- The same-seed repeat and the data-seed-1 run are +77 and +70 of 855 against the BF16 twin (+9.01 and +8.19 points). Each is higher on 10 of 11 tasks and tied on one. Against the original FP32 run they are −2 and −9 of 855; the data-seed-1 run is also −7 against the repeat and +60 against 10/05.
- At 5e-6, FP32 against its BF16 twin: −10/855 (−1.17 points), descriptive, one trained checkpoint per policy at 5e-6.
- Across the three observed G20-fp32 exports the pooled scores were 293, 291 and 284 of 855, each above the 214/855 G20r2 result.
- The CPU data-path audit for the data-seed-1 run found zero shared full-example fingerprints among its 439 general rows, and confirmed the same 41 edit-call packs at the same positions and the same model seed. Multi-host loader execution was unverified.

### Limits

- These are eval-r2 edit-call scores from one checkpoint per training run and BF16 serving weights. Micro210 is the planned broader check on the original export.
- The FP32 policy changed parameter, gradient and optimizer-state dtypes together, so no single dtype is isolated.
- The three G20-fp32 runs at 2e-5 used the same model seed.
- Exact added-row task and file overlap was zero. Exposure through the general mix, including the data-seed-1 run's new general sample, remains unverified, as does task and TMax exposure inherited from the base data.
- The 10/05 seed-0 and greedy results came from an earlier serve. Its pooled seeds 1–5 came from a separate noise-only serve. The G20 and G5 seed-0, greedy and pooled results share a serve within each export. Each checkpoint was served once under its listed setup. The 2e-5 FP32-policy arm has three training runs; the BF16-policy comparator has one.
- The zero-rate observation is endpoint-only, one group, one run per condition.
- Export manifest shard hashes are producer assertions unless independently rehashed.

### What runs next

- The 60-update FP32 pair was cleared at 20:52:44 UTC on 2026-11-18 and both jobs were submitted at 20:53 UTC. The control is general-only; the treatment replaces 164 of 1,920 packed rows with 41 E12-B packs and 123 TMax packs. The schedule holds 2e-5 through update 4,275, including all 60 updates. At 45 seconds per update the fast-path estimate is about 45 minutes of training-step time per arm, with first-step and other overhead extra.
- Micro210 is planned on the original G20-fp32 BF16 export.

### Links

- [Issue 11646](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11646): first expert-MuonH train step stalls on 64 H100s
- [Issue 11536](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536): Snowball writes malformed JSON in nested Pi edit calls
- [Issue 11539](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11539): Snowball SFT with vs without TMax agent traces
- Parent: [issue 11535](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535)

🤖 **Snowball SFT line of work (2026-11-17 to 2026-11-19): data, scale against 10/05, recipes, results, and limits.**

## 1. TL;DR

- **One-hour FP32 edit-call:** treatment (`E12-B + TMax`, 60 updates, LR `2e-5`, fresh state) scored `337/855` (`.394`) on `eval-r2` versus `222/855` (`.260`) for its matched general-only control (`+13.45` pp, higher on all 11 tasks; [one-hour edit-call comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6996439113)).
- **One-hour FP32 Micro210:** over two repeats of one export per arm, treatment averaged `39.47%` suite and `14.99%` agent versus `41.59%` suite and `20.00%` agent for control (`−2.13` / `−5.01` pp; missing-outcome bounds `−2.96` to `−1.25` / `−8.45` to `−0.95` pp; control repeats differed by `3.06` / `6.32` pp).
- **BF16 stored-parameter finding:** 26 finished ablation runs and 4 short diagnostics trained with `params=bfloat16` and `master_param_mode=device` ([BF16 inventory](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6999152021)); [draft PR 11717](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11717) enforces FP32 stored parameters.
- **Status at the 04:49Z update on November 19:** `control`, `single`, and `Warm A` were training. Slow `repeat` was cancelled (`04:46:32Z` readback: killed); `repeat-r2` did not launch. `Warm B` was still queued at the latest placement readback (`0/8`). `Warm A control` was cleared under the new rule: continuations from 10/05 carry optimizer state and use the cooled-down LR; fresh state is reserved for starts from the pretrained base.

## 2. Data

| Set | Construction and size | Loss mask and supervised targets |
|---|---|---|
| **General packs** | Rows sampled from the replay of the 10/05 mix, in a fixed order within each frozen row schedule (`262,144` positions/pack; 1,927 text-format components including agentic sources; full 10/05 mix is `79.65%` SFT + `20.35%` pretraining replay; `data_seed=1` changes the general sample and order). | Full-text causal loss (from config, trainer source, and CPU row audit; no prompt mask; S3 general cache weights were not re-read directly). Planned eight-hour control CPU row-proof count: `3,779,290,292` targets over `15,360` packs (`93.86%` of positions, ~`246k`/pack). |
| **E12-B** | Programmatic exercises from TMax train-split code bodies with one to four corrupted regions, with one Pi 0.87 nested `edit` call as the target (`5,536` exercises / `724` tasks / `41` packs; `5,536/5,536` exact Pi 0.87.0 pure-edit matches; `0` overlap with `eval-r1`/`eval-r2` tasks). | **Final edit call only:** `2,176,018` targets over `10,579,547` real positions (`20.6%` of real positions; `20.25%` of `41 × 262,144` padded positions; mean `53,074`/pack). |
| **TMax** | Successful Qwen3.6-27B mini-swe-agent traces from `allenai/tmax-sft` (`9d6ab747`, thinking split). Full train source pool: `4,647` traces / `909` tasks / `129` packs (`900` of those `4,647` source-pool traces were already in 10/05; `507` / `101` held out). Selected for one-hour and eight-hour arms: packs `0–122` (`123` packs, `4,512` traces; packs `123–128` excluded). | **Full-trace causal loss:** within each trace, each position has weight `1` except the final EOS position, which has weight `0`. The weight at position `k` supervises token `k+1`, so this mask excludes the transition to the next trace. Across selected packs `0–122`: `31,605,382` targets of `31,609,894` non-pad positions (`98.02%` of padded positions; mean `256,954`/pack): assistant `47.5%` (`15.01M`), tool outputs `33.4%` (`10.57M`), user `13.9%` (`4.39M`), system + tool schemas `3.9%` (`1.23M`), role headers `1.3%` (`0.41M`). Matches general packs' full-text loss except each TMax trace excludes its transition across final EOS. (Measured on rendered traces and cache audit; independent technical read in progress.) |

Planned-schedule CPU row-proof shares for combined `E12-B + TMax` arms (`164` packs = `41` E12-B + `123` TMax, `33,781,400` targets): one-hour treatment substitutes `164/1,920` rows (`8.54%` of rows, `7.26%` of its `465,505,869` planned targets); eight-hour `single` substitutes `164/15,360` rows (`1.07%` of rows, `0.90%` of planned targets); eight-hour `repeat` substitutes `1,312/15,360` rows (`164 × 8`, `8.54%` of rows, `7.25%` of planned targets). For `Warm A` and queued `Warm B`, `7.25%` is the repeat-schedule projection, not consumed data.

## 3. Scale against 10/05 SFT

Formula: Levanter `lm_flops_per_token` (non-causal full-span attention convention) for Snowball (`hidden=2560`, `intermediate=1280`, `shared=2560`, `layers=26`, `heads=20`, `kv_heads=5`, `vocab=128,256`, `256` experts, top-4, `sliding_window=2048`, `7` full-attention layers per `_long_layer_schedule(26, 4)` — layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25 — matching the 10/05 W&B analytic value `23,911,178,240` forward FLOPs/token). Training FLOPs = `3 × 23,911,178,240 × positions` (`7.173353e10` FLOPs/position; `6.02e17` FLOPs per 32-pack update).

| Run scale | Updates | Packs / update | Positions (`× 262,144`) | Training FLOPs (`3×` analytic) | Share of 10/05 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **10/05 SFT** (step `157,000 → 161,750`) | `4,750` | `256` | `318.77B` (`318,767,104,000`) | `2.29e22` | `100%` |
| **15-update arms** (per arm: `C-*`, `G*`) | `15` | `32` | `0.126B` (`125,829,120`) | `9.03e18` | `0.0395%` (`1/2,533`) |
| **One-hour pair** (scheduled per arm) | `60` | `32` | `0.503B` (`503,316,480`) | `3.61e19` | `0.1579%` (`1/633`) |
| **Eight-hour arms** (scheduled per arm) | `480` | `32` | `4.027B` (`4,026,531,840`) | `2.89e20` | `1.2632%` (`1/79.2`) |

## 4. Recipe facts per run family

All 11-17 to 11-19 arms below use `seq=262,144`, `bs=32`, Mochi grouping (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`, `global_grad_norm=1.0`, `weight_decay=0.0`, special-token LR `√32 × LR`), and BF16 compute/output.

| **10/05 SFT (reference)** | Pre-train base `step-157000` (native FP32) | Carried base state | `5e-5` peak (no warmup), final ~475-step decay to `0.1×` (saved scalar `5.094738e-6`) | FP32 | `4,750` (`bs=256`) |
| **Carried BF16** (`C-replay r3`, `C-e12`) | 10/05 native `step-161750` | Carried | `5e-6` constant | BF16 | `15` |
| **G0 / G5 / G20 BF16** (`G0r2`, `G5r2`, `G20r2`) | 10/05 BF16 native import (`step-0`) | Fresh | `0` / `5e-6` / `2e-5` constant | BF16 | `15` |
| **G5 / G20 FP32** (`G5-fp32 r2`; `G20-fp32 r3`, `rep r1`, `ds1 r1`) | 10/05 BF16-upcast-to-FP32 (`step-0`) | Fresh | `5e-6` / `2e-5` constant | FP32 | `15` |
| **One-hour FP32 pair** (`control`, `treatment`) | 10/05 BF16-upcast-to-FP32 (`step-0`) | Fresh | `2e-5` constant | FP32 | `60` |
| **Eight-hour FP32 fresh** (`control`, `single`, `repeat`) | 10/05 BF16-upcast-to-FP32 (`step-0`) | Fresh | `2e-5` through update `432`, then the `48`-update linear decay schedule; the last applied LR is `2.375e-6` (the configured floor is `2e-6`) | FP32 | `480` |
| **Eight-hour Warm A** (`repeat` mix; `Warm A control` general-only) | 10/05 native `step-161750` (FP32) | Carried FP32 | `5.094738e-6` constant | FP32 | `480` |
| **Eight-hour Warm B** (`repeat` mix) | 10/05 native `step-161750` (FP32) | Carried FP32 | `2e-5` through update `432`, then the `48`-update linear decay schedule; the last applied LR is `2.375e-6` (the configured floor is `2e-6`) | FP32 | `480` |

**Eight-hour status (2026-11-19 04:05Z–04:49Z):** `control` (`116` updates @ `45.0` s/upd at ~04:13Z) and `single` (`81` @ `45.1` s at ~04:13Z) were training fast; `Warm A` was training (`15` updates by 04:05Z, `72/72` arrays restored and `36/36` FP32 moment audits passed). Slow `repeat` (`62+` updates @ `125.7` s) was cancelled (readback `04:46:32Z`: killed), and `repeat-r2` did not launch. `Warm B` remained queued at the latest placement readback (`0/8`). `Warm A control` (general-only, carried FP32, `5.094738e-6`) was cleared at `04:49Z`.

## 5. Results so far

**Edit-call (`eval-r2`, 5-seed pooled, `855` replies/arm):**
- **Carried BF16 step-15:** `C-e12` `.263` (within-serve seeds `41–50/171`) versus `C-replay r3` `.271` (`43–53/171`) and `10/05` `.262` (`40–48/171`; all BF16-parameter continuations marked in [BF16 inventory](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6999152021)).

| **1h treatment − control** | `−5.01` pp (control spread `6.32` pp) | `−8.45` to `−0.95` pp | `−2.13` pp (control spread `3.06` pp) | `−2.96` to `−1.25` pp |
| **10/05 parent** (`44627` / `44628`, prior table; parity unverified) | `20.10%` (`100/100`) / `19.16%` (`93/100`) | — | `41.44%` (`440/440`) / `40.91%` (`433/440`) | — |
| **Carried BF16 step-15** (`C-replay r3` `44640/41`; `C-e12` `44642/43`) | `15.63%` / `21.12%`; `16.36%` / `20.41%` | — | `39.29%` / `43.43%`; `39.13%` / `38.85%` | — |

**Held-out retention loss (one-hour FP32, updates 15 / 30 / 45 / 60):** treatment `0.495105 / 0.494793 / 0.495092 / 0.495328` versus control `0.494975 / 0.494503 / 0.494595 / 0.494820` (within `0.00051` nats at every check; [one-hour edit-call comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6996439113)).

**Earlier `2e-5` BF16 runs are confounded:** the earlier E12 pilot control and treatment ([issue 11536](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536)) scored below 10/05 on Micro210. In the TMax comparison ([issue 11539](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11539)), both continuations scored below their parent on BFCL ×5 under both evaluated serve stacks. These continuations used fresh optimizer state, BF16 stored parameters, and LR `2e-5`, so the results cannot assign the drops to any one of those factors. Earlier pretrained-base screens ([issue 11537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11537), C150/O150) also used BF16 stored parameters at `2e-5` with fresh state from the pretrained base (so their gaps to 10/05 are not drops from their initializer) and need an FP32 redo.

## 6. Limits and Next

- **Limits:** (1) Eight-hour readouts are still in progress; current Micro210 results are two repeats of one export per one-hour arm. The one-hour Micro210 direction is lower for treatment on both metrics even under the missing-outcome bounds, while two repeats leave evaluation variability and training-seed effects unresolved. (2) Treatment arms bundle E12-B and TMax together, so their individual contributions are not separated, and TMax uses full-trace loss rather than assistant-only loss. (3) The `G20-fp32` checks include a same-seed rerun and a run with a different general-data seed. All three used the same model seed, so model-seed variation remains unmeasured; all other arms have one training run per condition. (4) The edit-call and Micro210 scores here describe the BF16 exports. For the one-hour edit-call pair, the added rows share `0` of `11` `eval-r2` task IDs, added-file overlap is unknown, and inherited 10/05 exposure is unverified. (5) Harness parity between the four one-hour Micro210 runs (`44652`, `44653`, `44658`, `44659`) and the earlier `10/05` parent runs (`44627–44628`) was not rechecked. (6) Nine known broader-suite import failures remain unresolved and outside the 20-source Micro210 results; they are not counted as passing.
- **Next:** Complete and score the active eight-hour arms (`control`, `single`, `Warm A`) at checkpoints `120 / 240 / 480`; run cleared `Warm A control` (general-only, carried FP32 state, `5.094738e-6`) to form a matched pair under the 04:44Z continuation rule; run queued `Warm B` (kept: with `Warm A` it isolates the learning rate under carried state); review Mochi weaknesses from existing evals before planning any larger FP32 base-start SFT run.

Control's held-out loss was flat: 0.49477 at the first check, 0.49449 at the last. Single-use was lower at all 8 checks by 0.00001 to 0.00007 nats. That is no measurable difference in held-out loss. Both runs finished with 480 finite training losses. Their BF16 copies are made. Exports and benchmark scores are not done yet.

## New design: runs from the pre-train base

All runs start from the pre-train base (the checkpoint that 10/05 SFT started from). They use fresh optimizer state, FP32 training, and 150 updates of 32 packs. Each arm changes one thing against the same control.

## One-hour runs that finished today

Both are 60-update runs from 10/05 with the one-hour pair's setup (fresh state, LR `2e-5`, FP32).

- All runs that continue SFT from 10/05, including any new carried-state, fresh-state or LR-restart runs

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Scope check: the BF16 stored-parameter bug is limited to runs launched from `experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft-smoke.yaml`. The upstream training lines all store FP32 parameters with BF16 compute:

| Line | Parameters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Snowball 67B-A2B pretraining (10T run, step-39k cooldown) | FP32 | The W&B consumed config of [`moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k) records `param_dtype=float32, compute_dtype=bfloat16, output_dtype=bfloat16`. Every launcher at pin `5681efbe3f` (branch `june_tpu_67b_a2b`) sets the same policy: base 10T, resume15k, cooldown and both YaRN variants. |
| Mochi hero pretraining and the 262K extension (`hero-lce-log65536sq-step390k`) | FP32 | `hero_recipe.py`: `MasterParamMode.DEVICE` maps to `params=float32,compute=bfloat16,output=bfloat16`. The README states "fp32 on device with bf16 compute". |
| Long-loop Exp3 and Exp4 production SFT | FP32 | `exp3_production.py` builds `p=f32,c=bfloat16`. `exp3_recipe.py:131` rejects any other policy when the recipe is built. |

Not yet checked against W&B: the Snowball 10T run before step 39k, and the 262K extension that produced `snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`. Both use the same launcher policy.

Probable cause of the bad line: `hero_recipe.py` defines `HERO_MIXED_PRECISION = "params=bfloat16,..."`. That policy is correct only with `MasterParamMode.FP32_PINNED_HOST`, where an FP32 master copy stays on the host. `sft-smoke.yaml` pairs `params=bfloat16` with `master_param_mode: device`. No FP32 copy exists anywhere in that combination, and no check rejects it. Suggested guard, in addition to #11717's one-line fix: make the SFT runtime reject `params=bfloat16` with `master_param_mode: device` when the config is built.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body: 🤖 Correction to my last comment: #11717 already adds the construction-time guard (`require_fp32_param_policy`), so it is more than a one-line YAML fix. The remaining suggestion, renaming the hero BF16 policy constant, is now on #11717.

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
### What

Implement Olympiad and Research as separate single-turn evaluations in TaskCompendium. On Olympiad, the judge checks whether the written answer is equivalent to the reference answer. On Research, it scores the solution against the item’s 10-point rubric. The pilot uses one answer per released row on each track. [Paper, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21165v1) · [Pinned dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/frontierscience/tree/25ed67db7da8f4591484e764008ff585544f5a30)

### Why

Can a model explain *how* it reached a scientific conclusion well enough to earn credit for the intermediate steps? GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro already test whether Marin can select the right answer. Olympiad adds short-answer physics, chemistry, and biology questions. FrontierScience-Research gives each written solution up to 10 rubric points, so we can see partial progress even when few answers reach the passing threshold. ByteDance used both pass rate and mean rubric points to compare Axion checkpoints during training. [Marin eval policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) · [Axion technical report](https://axion1-0.github.io/paper/axion.pdf)

### Decisions for review

| Decision | OpenAI’s published evaluation | Marin pilot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Population | The gold set has 100 Olympiad and 60 Research rows. The paper does not say how its runner handled the duplicate Research problem. | Use all released rows. Report Research pass rate over 60 rows as primary. Also report the rate after excluding the second duplicate (row 12) and the percentage-point difference. |
| Trials | OpenAI averaged accuracy over 20 independent trials per Olympiad question and 30 per Research question. | Generate one response per row. Report a standard error across problems for each track, preserving subject mix and grouping the duplicate Research rows during resampling. One draw per row cannot measure run-to-run variation on the fixed release. |
| Solver | Reasoning models used high effort, except GPT-5.2 at xhigh. Browsing was disabled. We found no numeric solver output cap in the release. | Send the released problem in one user turn, with thinking enabled and no tools or retrieval. Qwen’s thinking switch has no established equivalence to OpenAI’s effort levels. |
| Judge and scores | GPT-5 at high effort checked answer equivalence for Olympiad and awarded rubric points for Research. Research passes at **7/10 or above**. | Use GPT-OSS-120B at high effort with the published Appendix B prompts. Give the judge the problem, visible final answer, and reference answer or rubric. Report Olympiad accuracy and Research pass rate separately. Also retain decimal rubric points and report their mean. |

For the full Qwen3.6-35B-A3B run, set the output cap to **81,920 tokens**, shared between reasoning and the final answer. Qwen recommends this cap for highly complex benchmarks independently of thinking mode. The SU-01 evaluation setup lists 131K tokens for Olympiad and 256K for Research. Record length stops by track so reviewers can judge whether the cap affected scores. [Qwen guidance](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B#best-practices) · [SU-01 evaluation settings](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.13301v1)

Use Qwen’s general-task thinking preset on both full tracks: `temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=20`, `min_p=0.0`, `presence_penalty=1.5`, and `repetition_penalty=1.0`. Equivalence to OpenAI’s original sampling settings is unverified. [Qwen model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B#best-practices)

For a solver length stop, grade the visible final-answer text. A correct Olympiad answer can earn full credit. A partial Research solution earns the rubric points it satisfies and passes at 7/10. Score zero if the solver produces no final-answer text. Keep length stops in the denominator and report them separately. Marin’s ID OlympiadBench scorer provides precedent for accepting a complete extractable answer when generation reaches its limit. Final-only extraction and partial Research rubric credit are explicit FrontierScience pilot choices. [ID policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) · [Pinned OlympiadBench scorer](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c1d5c62cdc3939b42f64411af44fd50716b53454/eval/chat_benchmarks/OlympiadBench/eval_instruct.py#L568-L581)

Set `EvaluationItem.groups["subject"]` from the source row so the run records contain both track headline scores and six subject scores, one for each track and subject. Compute each headline across the released rows to preserve the published subject mix. In the validation PR, link the run records and show the correct or passing count, graded count, and expected population alongside each score. Verify coverage with `cli scores`. [Subject reporting, Figure 7](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21165v1#S3.SS1) · [Marin subgroup reporting](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/139b752890/docs/tutorials/add-evaluation.md#L130-L138)

See [published settings and aggregation, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21165v1#S3.SS1) · [judge prompt, Appendix B](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/2fcd284c-b468-4c21-8ee0-7a783933efcc/frontierscience-paper.pdf) · [dataset discussion of the duplicate](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/frontierscience/discussions/3).

### Validation

**Source checked.** The dataset card lists Apache-2.0. At revision `25ed67db7da8f4591484e764008ff585544f5a30`, Olympiad contains 50 physics, 40 chemistry, and 10 biology rows. [Pinned Olympiad file](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/frontierscience/blob/25ed67db7da8f4591484e764008ff585544f5a30/olympiad/test.jsonl)

Research contains 20 rows per subject, 59 distinct problem texts, and 59 distinct source task IDs. Physics rows 7 and 12 (one-based) match in every field. Assign a stable execution ID to each track and row, retaining the original task ID for provenance. Verify that both rows are sampled independently, that cached results cannot substitute one for the other, and that resuming preserves each row’s own response and grade. The 59-problem sensitivity score reuses these grades. [Pinned Research file](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/frontierscience/blob/25ed67db7da8f4591484e764008ff585544f5a30/research/test.jsonl)

**Implementation and runs are pending.** Check the compiled populations against the source counts and test Olympiad equivalence verdicts. Verify the compiled solver prompts against the pinned rows and the judge prompts against Appendix B. Check the full-run solver request payloads against the agreed sampling preset, thinking flag, and output cap. Verify that the outgoing judge request selects GPT-OSS-120B with high effort. Record the returned model identity and judge output budget. Test scores below, exactly at, and above 7 and distinguish malformed judge output from a scientific answer earning zero.

1. Smoke-test 50 rows from each track with Qwen3-0.6B. Confirm that all selected rows receive a grade and resolve infrastructure failures.
2. Run Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on both full tracks with one response per row. Reuse the external Qwen checkpoint that [Marin evaluated alongside Snowball](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/139b752890/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/model-configs/Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.yaml), `995ad96eacd98c81ed38be0c5b274b04031597b0`. Prefer item-level agreement. If only aggregate scores are available, report each track’s score and uncertainty alongside the reference, naming differences in judge, trials, and solver settings. Record expected and graded counts, truncations, and judge failures.
3. Inspect at least 20 graded responses and every unparseable case. For the grader audit, freeze a sample from both tracks and have two reviewers independently grade the same saved answers, blinded to the pilot verdict and each other. Include randomly selected responses as well as equivalent Olympiad answers and Research scores near 7. Record sampling strata and weights, disagreement on passes, and differences in rubric points. Report malformed judge outputs as grading failures. [Add-eval workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/add-eval/SKILL.md) · [Grader audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/audit-grader/SKILL.md)

Two teams published scores for the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B baseline. Neither team's exact weights revision has been verified against Marin’s pin.

| Source | Olympiad | Research | How the team reported the score |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| [SU-01, Tables 1–2](https://huggingface.co/Simplified-Reasoning/SU-01#evaluation) | 65.0% | 5.0% | Olympiad averages four runs. SU-01 describes rule-based checks followed by GPT-OSS-120B for unresolved Olympiad answers, and GPT-5-high for Research. Research repeat count is unverified. [Grading details, Appendix G](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.13301v1#A7) |
| [ByteDance Axion, §4.1 and Table 2](https://axion1-0.github.io/paper/axion.pdf) | 71.0% | 26.7% | Best complete run of three. The harness supports tools under benchmark-specific restrictions. Qwen’s actual tool use on these tracks is unverified. |

The 21.7-point gap on Research makes either aggregate a weak test of grader correctness. Where reference grades are available, compare verdicts on the same saved answers.

### Cost

The full one-trial run produces **100 Olympiad and 60 Research responses**, with one grade per row. At the chosen cap, that permits up to 13,107,200 solver output tokens across the full run. The published repeat counts imply **2,000 Olympiad and 1,800 Research responses** per model at the released track sizes. The separate Qwen smoke adds 50 responses and grades per track, bringing the planned total to 260 solver responses and 260 row grades before retries or audit regrading. Empty final answers can receive zero without a judge call. Runtime and spend remain unmeasured.

### Remaining scope

Configure the serving context to fit the longest rendered prompt plus 81,920 output tokens. The earlier Marin comparison run used a 73,728-token total context. Consider EvalDash presentation when reviewing the benchmark for ID policy admission.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

No open PR targets FrontierScience. TaskCompendium derives task IDs from source provenance, including the row locator, so the duplicate Research rows can retain separate execution identities. Three requested Qwen sampling fields are absent from the evaluation protocol, the current Qwen3.6 serve config has a 32,768-token context, and Verifyit's judge has no continuous 0–10 rubric score; these require implementation before the full pilot.

**Relevant code**
- [Task ID derivation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4e4a35f8ae68a8a5a76626f2f323f16dabbd881d/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/conversion.py#L37) — includes the source row.
- [Evaluation protocol](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4e4a35f8ae68a8a5a76626f2f323f16dabbd881d/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/evaluation/spec.py#L162) — sampling and metrics contract.
- [Request serialization](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4e4a35f8ae68a8a5a76626f2f323f16dabbd881d/lib/marin/src/marin/rollouts/evaluation.py#L115) — sends current sampling fields.
- [Judge contract](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4e4a35f8ae68a8a5a76626f2f323f16dabbd881d/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/spec.py#L314) — fixed labels and checklist scoring.
- [Qwen serve config](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4e4a35f8ae68a8a5a76626f2f323f16dabbd881d/experiments/evaluation/serve/models/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.yaml#L1) — current context limit.

## Proposed Fix

1. Add source converters for `olympiad/test.jsonl` and `research/test.jsonl` at revision `25ed67db7da8f4591484e764008ff585544f5a30`, with separate benchmark declarations. Preserve each released row's locator and original task ID in evidence; set `groups["subject"]`, `final_only` response selection, one trial, and independent headline metrics. Register both in the curated catalog. Test the 100/60 populations, subject counts, and two independent Research duplicate IDs and grades through resume.
2. Reproduce the Appendix B judge prompts. Implement Olympiad equivalence on the judge path; add a strictly parsed decimal 0–10 Research score that records rubric points and a pass at `>=7`. Keep malformed judge output as a grading failure and an empty solver final answer as scored zero. Bind GPT-OSS-120B with high reasoning effort and retain the returned model identity and judge budget.
3. Represent `min_p`, presence penalty, and repetition penalty in the typed sampling contract and outgoing request. Verify the full Qwen payload, including `temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=20`, thinking enabled, and the 81,920-token output cap. Pin the Qwen checkpoint and set serving context from the longest rendered prompt plus that cap; require context admission to preserve the full allowance.

issues.author: Helw150
issues.body:
Hard benchmarks, especially agentic tasks, require large base models before downstream scores become useful. This makes a closed loop of pretraining, posttraining, and evaluation undoably expensive (even just the last two steps are expensive!). The goal is to assess whether hints on smaller models provide enough signal to guide SFT recipe improvements using extremely small proxy models.

Not set in stone, but seems reasonable to use [Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) as the larger, post-emergence checkpoint for validation.

## Starting points

- The new pretraining scaling ladder from Larry in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9287
- The existing [hint-based estimation work](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4549).
- The [evaluation policies](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9113).

## What this builds

Augment the new pretraining ladder with corresponding SFT path. Implements hint-assisted evaluation as reusable code that plugs into the existing evalchemy based evaluation tooling and the ladder. Start with hard, preferably agentic tasks, expanding to all tasks in the eval policy if there is time!

Assess how the hinted scores relate to unassisted performance on the larger checkpoint. Use that evidence to judge whether the method provides a useful signal for recipe selection.

Use hint-assisted scoring to develop and test a new SFT recipe expected to produce stronger results. Compare it with the initial recipe across the ladder and explain what the measurements support about its expected larger-scale performance.

What done looks like

- [ ] The pretraining ladder has corresponding SFT checkpoints, with reproducible training configurations.
- [ ] Hint-assisted evaluation is implemented and runs across the ladder, alongside unhinted baselines.
- [ ] The relationship between ladder scores and the larger checkpoint’s unassisted performance is measured and reported.
- [ ] Hint-assisted scores have informed at least one SFT recipe iteration, with a comparison against the initial recipe.
- [ ] A writeup assesses predictive value, uncertainty, accelerator cost, and whether the scoring method is useful for selecting SFT recipes.
- [ ] Code, configurations, and results are available to reproduce the experiments.

The outcome is an assessment of viability. Report failures and inconclusive results as well as improvements.

Out of scope

- RL.
- Changing the scaling ladder’s underlying training implementation.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The likely ladder is the four-rung `experiments/grug/fast_track` MoE ladder tracked in [#9451](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451). Its published runs do not by default retain permanent checkpoints, and its 16k tokenizer and KDA/MLA architecture differ from the named [67B SFT checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) (128k vocabulary, 256 experts). The prior [pass@k study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4549) establishes a hint/scaffold motivation, but its reported solution-primed GSM8K score saturated at pass@32; it does not establish that hints rank SFT recipes on hard agentic tasks. [#9537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9537) has a one-example serving smoke test for the 67B checkpoint, while chat reasoning extraction remains untested. [#9348](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9348) studies student-guided SFT data selection, a related but distinct question; I found no open PR implementing this hint-evaluation study.

**Relevant code**
- [`fast_track/launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py#L254-L269) — rung and checkpoint controls.
- [`fast_track/train.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/grug/fast_track/train.py#L196-L217) — model-specific training data path.
- [`sft/launcher.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/sft/launcher.py) — reusable SFT specification and chat masking.
- [`evaluation/README.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/evaluation/README.md) — shared Evalchemy/Harbor launcher and records.

# Proposed Fix

1. **Freeze the comparison.** Inventory which d512/d768/d1024/d1280 pretraining checkpoints exist; rerun missing rungs with `--save-checkpoints`. Pin their commits, data, tokenizer, model configs, and checkpoint URIs. Choose one initial SFT recipe aligned with [#8089](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8089), including immutable data revisions, chat template, loss mask, step/token budget, seed, and export contract. Keep the pretraining ladder implementation unchanged.
2. **Make one rung end to end.** Adapt the `fast_track` model to the existing SFT data path, with a weights-only start and completion-token loss, then export and serve one d512 checkpoint. Verify unhinted evaluation and stored per-task samples before training all four rungs. Keep SFT/backend and serving changes in reviewable PRs separate from evaluation policy changes.
3. **Add versioned hints to the evaluation tooling.** Start with a fixed hard Harbor panel from the [current eval policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9409), such as TBLite/TB2 and SWE-bench Verified random-100. Define no-hint and at least two fixed hint strengths per task, record the hint source and text with each sample, and keep the agent, generation settings, verifier, task IDs, and attempt budget identical. Audit hints for answer leakage; add behavioral tests for hint injection and result identity. Extend to Evalchemy tasks only after the agentic pilot works.
4. **Run the matrix.** Evaluate the initial SFT recipe at all four rungs with and without hints, then choose one changed SFT recipe using a development task split and retrain all rungs at matched SFT compute. Score both recipes on held-out tasks with the same policy and seeds. Run the named 67B checkpoint unhinted on those tasks after chat-mode serving is verified. Publish run IDs, checkpoint/config revisions, per-task outcomes, failures, training GPU-hours, inference tokens/GPU-hours, and Harbor sandbox cost.
5. **Test predictive value.** On held-out tasks, compare hinted small-model scores with the 67B unhinted scores and with the cheaper small-model unhinted baseline. Report task-paired bootstrap intervals, rank agreement across rungs, recipe deltas, saturation, and cost per discriminating comparison. A single 67B recipe cannot validate a *recipe uplift* prediction at 67B; unless a matched second large-checkpoint recipe is available, report the larger-scale recipe conclusion as a hypothesis with that limitation explicit.

The first decision gate is an end-to-end d512 run: if checkpoint export/serving or non-leaking hints fail, resolve those before spending on the full ladder. Treat the 16k-to-128k tokenizer and architecture change as an external-validity limit even if the task-level correlations are positive.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
On 64 H100 (CoreWeave cw-us-east-02a, JAX 0.11.1, Snowball e12 FP32 SFT, 8x8 mesh, `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`), the same `jit_train_step` executable runs at about 122 s/step in the process that compiled it, and at about 45 s/step in a fresh process that loads it from the persistent JAX compilation cache. The cause is not known.

**Evidence**

| Run | Cache | Steady step |
|---|---|---:|
| Controlled pre-job (3 updates, empty cache) | miss, compile 14.2 s | 125.7, 122.5 s |
| Same config, next job, same cache URI | hit, 2.6 s | 49.4, 41.7, 44.4, 46.8 s |
| Distillation arm A, alpha 0 (compiled in-process; cache entry `jit_train_step-a19e8a54…`) | miss | 122 s (MFU 6.9%) |
| Same code and config, new job | hit on `a19e8a54…` (no new entry written) | 44.6, 41.2, 42.4, 47.4, 47.0, 38.1 s |

- The controlled test used one cache key, `jit_train_step-61378ece…`, in both stages. The executable fingerprint and compiled-text SHA256 match.
- The slow process is GPU-bound: ~350 of 411 s of a 3-step trace is on the compute stream, and ~100 s/step is in Triton GEMM fusions with small tiles (block 64, 768 B shared memory).
- Ruled out: autotune level (the fast program was also compiled at level 0, and the cached copy is the same executable), the per-fusion autotune cache (the cached autotune sets for the slow and fast trees match on 131,051 of 131,072 sampled keys), checkpointing, row content, and code version.
- Autotune level 4 was tried once: the compile finished in 41 s, but no step completed in 2.5 h (separate hang, not diagnosed).
- Compile records:
  - miss: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-fp32-redo-20261119/mochi-5cb/control-compile-prejob/compile-record.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-fp32-redo-20261119%2Fmochi-5cb%2Fcontrol-compile-prejob%2Fcompile-record.json))
  - hit: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-fp32-redo-20261119/mochi-5cb/control/compile-record.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-fp32-redo-20261119%2Fmochi-5cb%2Fcontrol%2Fcompile-record.json))
- Profile trace of the slow process: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/xprof/task504-distill-b-soft-20261119-profile/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Ftask504-distill-b-soft-20261119-profile%2F))

**Why it matters**

The first run of any new config (code change, new schedule, new data shapes) compiles its own step and runs ~3x slower for its whole length. A config that differs from a warmed template looks 3x slower without anyone noticing why.

**Workaround**

Run a short warm-up job first: the same config, stopped after 3 updates, on the same `JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR`. Then start the real run and check that no new `jit_train_step` entry is written, or look for `Persistent compilation cache hit for 'jit_train_step'`.

**Open question**

What differs between the compiling process and a loading process? Candidates include a kernel choice made at compile time and then replaced on load, memory placement or allocator state left by compilation, and leftover autotuning buffers. A profile of both processes on the same executable would show which kernels differ.

Found by duiker (controlled test) and otter (task 504). Related: PR 11732.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The controlled cache miss and hit use the same `jit_train_step` cache key and executable fingerprint, yet steady steps take about 122 and 42–49 seconds. The available device trace covers only the slow process, so it cannot show whether the fast process runs different kernels or runs the same kernels faster. The Long Loop step is one donated JIT call; related slow steps in #11646 do not establish a shared cause.

**Relevant code**
- [`train.py#L1264-L1280`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/454902f11d08aaaf89bb8b177896a533aabb6db5/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L1264-L1280) — donated JIT step.
- [`train.py#L1743-L1771`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/454902f11d08aaaf89bb8b177896a533aabb6db5/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L1743-L1771) — optional AOT compile before dispatch.
- [`launch_arms.py#L61-L86`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/454902f11d08aaaf89bb8b177896a533aabb6db5/experiments/post_training/teacher_distill/launch_arms.py#L61-L86) — shared remote cache setup.
- [`launch_arms.py#L112-L119`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/454902f11d08aaaf89bb8b177896a533aabb6db5/experiments/post_training/teacher_distill/launch_arms.py#L112-L119) — bounded profile and warm-up runs.

# Proposed Fix

1. On the same 8×8 H100 geometry, run a short cache-miss job followed by a cache-hit job with pinned source, image, `XLA_FLAGS`, input shapes, and cache URI. Record at least three unprofiled steady steps in each. Verify the cache key, executable fingerprint, and optimized HLO match before interpreting timing.
2. Capture two or three steady XPlane steps from each process at the same relative update. Compare kernel names, launch counts, GEMM tile choices, per-kernel duration, compute/collective time, and idle gaps with `profile_summary.py`. Confirm profiling preserves the slow/fast ordering; the existing slow-only trace cannot make this comparison.
3. If kernel choices differ, inspect XLA compile/load and autotune decisions. If choices match but runtimes differ, compare `cuda_async` allocator state, scratch availability, module-load activity, and direct compiled-executable versus stock JIT dispatch. Keep the executable and workload fixed while changing one runtime condition at a time.
4. Patch the isolated cause in Marin or report a minimal JAX/XLA replay upstream. Qualify a fix with repeated short miss/hit pairs, finite losses, no new cache entry on hits, and a steady-step gap below 10%.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Verifyit declares `requires-python = ">=3.11"` (`lib/verifyit/pyproject.toml`), and its runtime imports `enum.StrEnum` (`lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/grade.py:15`, `spec.py:17`, and four grade modes) and `tomllib` (`spec.py:15`, `modes/grade_json_schema.py:15`). The task-curation grading harness runs the staged runtime through the grader machine's own `python3` (`taskcompendium.runtime.grading._verifyit_reward`), so every grader machine below Python 3.11 fails grading with an import error instead of a verdict.

Task-curation workspace tasks whose source environment lowers onto a Python 3.10 base hit this at rollout: the Daytona census validates the machines, setup completes, and then the verifier returns `infra_error`:

```
File "/tests/.taskcompendium-runtime/verifyit/grade.py", line 15, in <module>
    from enum import StrEnum
ImportError: cannot import name 'StrEnum' from 'enum' (/usr/local/lib/python3.10/enum.py)
```

This affects the DCAgent python-tests family, where 7 of 10 sources lower onto `python:3.10-slim` bases (curriculum-easy, pymethods2test and its large cut, unitsyn-python and its large cut, e2egit and its large cut); their workspace-image graders run the image's Python 3.10.

Reproduce:
1. Convert a real `DCAgent__exp_rpt_curriculum-easy` row through `convert_python_tests` (the grader environment inherits the workspace image).
2. Grade an empty submission with `grade_empty_in_sandbox` against a Docker machine created from `RegistryImage(grader.docker_image)`.
3. Observe `infra_error` with the `StrEnum` import error above; on Python 3.11+ bases the same path returns `graded` with reward 0.0.

Expected: verifyit's runtime runs and returns a verdict on the grader machines the catalog's declared environments produce, including Python 3.10 workspace images, or the catalog refuses to declare a grader machine whose interpreter cannot run the runtime.

Evidence: end-to-end run over real TaskTrove rows on 2026-11-19 (multifile python:3.11 and stack-pytest/nl2bash ubuntu:24.04 graders return graded verdicts; the 3.10 cases stop at the import).

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 Candidate inference starts before a hosted judge's checkpoint is prepared. With a warm candidate and a cold judge, candidate accelerators remain reserved while the judge's CPU prepare job downloads its checkpoint.

Prepare the candidate and hosted judge checkpoints together before starting either inference service. Preserve independent serving configurations, immutable model revisions, and target-cluster/region cache placement. A preparation failure should prevent accelerator submission for both services.

Done when a regression test starts with a warm candidate and cold hosted judge and shows both preparation steps finish before either serving job is submitted.

Follow-up to https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10277#discussion_r4519907770 and #9233.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

[`run_evaluation_steps`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L602-L672) opens the candidate inference session before it constructs the hosted judge config. In [PR #10277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10277), each `remote_inference` call prepares its model and then submits its accelerator job, so a cold judge prepares while the warm candidate is already serving. That PR owns this code path and remains open for review.

**Relevant code**
- [`runner.py#L648-L671`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L648-L671) — candidate starts before judge config
- [`iris.py#L732-L759`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L732-L759) — preparation precedes serving per session
- [`iris.py#L783-L830`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L783-L830) — prepare jobs inherit each model's placement

# Proposed Fix

Extend #10277 so the eval runner constructs both inference configs, pins each Hugging Face revision, submits both sets of CPU preparation jobs to their respective serving placements, and waits for every preparation result before opening either inference session. Keep the candidate and judge serving configs independent; on any preparation error, terminate outstanding prepare jobs, record the infrastructure failure, and submit no accelerator jobs. Add a regression using a warm candidate and cold hosted judge that observes both preparations completing before either serving submission, plus a judge-preparation failure case. This belongs on #10277 rather than a parallel implementation PR.

spillover_issues.author: asartran
spillover_issues.body:
The marin unit test `tests/rl/test_rl_launch_documents.py::test_rl_launch_documents_load_with_the_vendored_launcher` takes 37 s at the median (55 s at p90, 114 s max) across 306 CI runs from Nov 15-18, which makes it one of the two slowest test files in the marin unit suite. CI deals test files to four marin shards, and the shard holding this file is often the last to finish, so it sets how long many PRs wait.

Almost all of that time is the SkyRL-side check, not the environment build. Timed on a development machine at `main` with a warm SkyRL environment:

| Stage | Time |
|---|---|
| Render the 103 launch documents (`render_launch_census`) | 5.5 s |
| SkyRL launcher subprocess loading the 103 documents (`tests/rl/launch_document_loader.py`) | 42.6 s |
| Build SkyRL's CPU environment from an empty uv cache | 10.9 s (0.5 s warm) |

Each `launch_config.load_launch_config` call composes the full SkyRL training config through Hydra (`_compose_source_recipe` -> `compose_skyrl_config` -> `hydra.compose`), with most of the time in OmegaConf deep copies, so the check costs about 0.4 s per document. It grows with every new launch document.

Done when:
- the test's CI time no longer grows with the number of launch documents, or stays under about 10 s on a GitHub `ubuntu-latest` runner, while still checking that every launch document loads with the vendored launcher (for example in the nightly slow job if not on every PR).

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** In an RL pass-rate screen on SWE-smith tasks, 575 of 1,024 Snowball tries had a broken tool call, and 524 of the 576 malformed spans were Pi `edit` calls. The 10/05 SFT data has almost no edit calls in Pi's nested shape.
- **Goal:** Stop Snowball from writing malformed JSON for Pi's nested `edit` tool by adding correct examples to its SFT data.
- **Data:** 1,000 synthetic Pi edit exercises built from open TMax code, each checked to restore the target file exactly, plus held-out exercises for testing. Later runs use a grown set of 5,536 exercises.
- **Method:** Short SFT runs from the 10/05 SFT with and without the slice, scored on a targeted eval (apply the model's edit and compare with the target file) and on Micro210.
- **Results:** In the FP32 from-base pair (one training run per arm), replacing 41 of 4,800 rows with edit-call exercises scored 120 of 855 on the edit-call test (higher on 10 of 11 tasks) and Micro210 score mass 97.39 / 99.33 (mean 98.36 of 440), against 63 of 855 and 87.30 / 87.28 (mean 87.29) for the control; native equal-20 overlapped across repeats (20.21% vs 19.12%), AIME24 and OlympiadBench accounted for 11.00 of the 11.07 mass points (the other 18 sources netted +0.07, with tool-use sources not clearly improving), and both arms sat far below the 2026-11-18 from-base control (145.01) and 10/05 (175.75). Earlier 15-update FP32 continuations from 10/05 scored 284 to 293 of 855 against 224 for 10/05 (issue 11687), and a partial Mochi screen found far fewer broken edit calls (7 of 358 against Snowball's 524 of 1,093) but ended undecided.
- **Conclusion:** On a weak baseline (one run per arm), the edit-data run scored nearly twice as high on the edit-call test with no measured cost to general ability, so we keep the edit-call rows in the mix. The effect size on a healthy model and any gain on real agent tasks are not yet measured, and earlier BF16 runs through 2026-11-18 carried the BF16 stored-parameter caveat (issue 11687).

## Description

Pi's edit tool takes `{"path": …, "edits": [{"oldText": …, "newText": …}, …]}`, a list of objects inside the arguments object. The 10/05 SFT data has about 2.7M flat `str_replace_editor(command, path, old_str, new_str)` calls and essentially no Pi-shape edits.

Measured in the screen above:
- 1,093 edit calls; 523 failed `json.loads`.
- 362 of the 524 broken edit spans parse after one insertion at the JSON error offset: `]}` for 259, `}` for 103. This is a syntax-only check. It does not show that the repaired edit applies or fixes the task.
- 14 of the 575 broken-call tries still scored 1, so a malformed final call does not always mean a failed task.

Examples are viewable without login in the public trace viewer: https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/ (run "Pass-rate 43604"). Missing `]}`: attempts [`010d96c8…`](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/#attempt=010d96c8bd03428fb13da34e880a3a73) (step 18) and [`0288247e…`](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/#attempt=0288247ea31c47e48cbb5c7ee3b6a467) (step 11). Missing `}`: [`04741406…`](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/#attempt=04741406ca5a4ff38401423e48ccd4ad) (step 18). The viewer shows only this screen and the edit-exercise training rows. It reads from temporary storage: the traces expire about 2026-11-28 and the exercise data about 2026-12-18, so the links are not durable.

An A/B with a flat replacement edit tool (16 tasks × 2 arms × 4 tries) solved 20/64 vs 7/64 for Pi's native tool. Malformed calls not caused by the output cap were 3 vs 25. A larger confirmation (128 tasks × 8 per arm) is pending review. Third-party harnesses fix their own tool schemas, so a flat tool would only help our own harness.

The SFT training data's tool calls are well-formed: 452 of 47,399,691 assistant call spans failed a delimiter and `json.loads` check, across 51 scanned sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The model learned the flat edit shape in SFT and miscounts brackets in Pi's nested shape. Adding valid nested-edit calls to SFT should cut the malformed-edit rate without lowering other scores.

## Status

- E12-B data built: 1,000 train / 100 val / 100 test synthetic Pi edit exercises from TMax code (ODC-BY), 1–4 edits per call, 393,750 supervised tokens in train. Each edit was checked to restore the target file exactly. [Manifest](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Farm-b-20261114-r1%2Fmanifest-r1.json) (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/arm-b-20261114-r1/manifest-r1.json`).
- 1 h version: three 15-update arms (general-only control, E12 full, E12 attention/head only) trained, exported and scored on Micro210. Results below.
- 8 h version: C150 recipe plus a grown E12-B set (~6k rows, at most 4 passes per row, about 0.8% of supervised tokens), against the existing C150 arm. It waits for the 1 h readout.
- Mochi: in its BFCL ×5 Pi traces, 1,445 tool calls parsed, and at most 3 messages left tool-call-like text unparsed. BFCL rarely uses `edit` (7 calls, none with more than one edit), so this does not test the nested-edit problem.

Readout: malformed-edit rate on Micro210's Pi trials, the Micro210 score paired by task, and the retention panel. Carry the slice into the next SFT stage if the malformed-edit rate falls by at least half against the matched control with no Micro210 or retention loss.

## Results (1 h version, as of 2026-11-17)

All three arms start from the 10/05 weights and run 15 updates of 32 × 262,144 tokens. In the two edit arms, the E12-B slice is 0.68% of supervised tokens: all 1,000 train exercises, seen twice. All Micro210 numbers are single runs; two runs of the parent differ by about 5 tasks (2.1 points).

| Model | Micro210, equal weight over 20 sources | vs parent run 1 | Held-out E12 edit loss (100 test rows, update 15) | Malformed `edit` spans in Micro210 Pi traces (about 100 records; one outlier record excluded) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10/05 parent, run 1 / repeat | 49.39 / 47.32 | 0 / −2.1 | not measured | 16 |
| General-only control | 43.57 | −5.8 | 0.0294 | 14 |
| E12 attention + head only | 46.52 | −2.9 | 0.0294 | 20 |
| E12 full | 42.48 | −6.9 | 0.0018 | 3 |

- **The control loses about as much as the full arm**, so the Micro210 drop comes from the continued training itself, not from the edit data. One untested difference: E12 restarted at LR 2e-5 with fresh optimizer moments, while 10/05 ended its decay at 5e-6. A rerun of the control at 5e-6 and a zero-update export control are being prepared.
- **The edit data taught the format only when all weights trained.** The full arm's held-out edit loss is 16× lower than the control's. The attention + head arm did not change.
- **Not shown yet:** that real edits improved. The malformed counts are witness counts, not rates. The excluded full-arm record alone holds 8,166 malformed spans (see the comment of 2026-11-17 07:34 UTC). A behavioral test is being built: each model answers the 100 held-out test prompts, and the returned edit is applied with Pi's edit function and checked against the target file.
- The pre-stated carry rule (malformed-edit rate at least halved, with no Micro210 or retention loss) is **not met**: the full arm loses 6.9 points.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-16: Do not train on the screen's own successful calls; those tasks are the readout panels.
- 2026-11-16: Keep Pi's native edit tool for reported benchmarks.

## Conclusion

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

The E12 arms are trained, and their Micro210 readout is pending. Plan:

1. Evaluate the control, full-slice, and attention/head arms on the same task and attempt set with the pinned Pi policy. Report malformed edit JSON failures per edit attempt, trials ending on a malformed call per trial, and output-cap truncations separately.
2. Publish paired Micro210 scores, scored and unscored counts, and retention results for each arm, with run and checkpoint IDs.
3. Apply the decision gate already stated in this issue. If an arm qualifies, compare the planned longer C150 treatment with its matched control, then record the result and recipe decision here.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Protocol FAIL; original preregistered confirmation claim FALSE.** The run completed, but the strict tool-contract check failed. The numbers below are descriptive, not a confirmed flat-edit effect or a promotion decision.

We compared Pi’s native nested edit arguments with a flat replacement on the same 128 SWE-smith training tasks, eight attempts per arm: 2,048 assignments. There were 2,024 verified binary outcomes and 24 masked/unknown outcomes, which were not counted as failures.

| Descriptive reading | Control wins / known | Flat wins / known | Complete task profiles | Flat-minus-control task-profile difference | Conditional 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| As recorded | 161 / 1,011 | 307 / 1,013 | 120 | **+14.38 percentage points** | +10.21 to +18.85 |
| Two affected attempts excluded | 161 / 1,011 | 305 / 1,011 | 118 | **+14.30 percentage points** | +9.96 to +18.75 |

The second reading removes two verified flat-arm wins from the pooled sensitivity only: nominal denominators become 1,024 control and 1,022 flat. The 13 control and 11 flat unknowns remain unknown. For the separate balanced eight-per-arm task comparison, the two affected task profiles become incomplete and are omitted; their other 30 outcomes remain pooled. The original endpoint is unchanged. These intervals condition on the observed complete task profiles; they do not cover excluded-task uncertainty, shared-run dependence, training-repeat variation or population generalization.

**Why strict confirmation failed:** two flat-arm attempts contained 65 requests using the native nested edit schema. Contracts were checked in 1,015 attempts per arm: zero affected control attempts and two affected flat attempts. Unchecked attempts and incomplete guard exposure are not assumed clean.

**Supported explanation:** in both cases, the outer agent ran `pi submit` through its bash tool. Pi 0.87 treats `submit` as a prompt, not a submission command. The resulting recorded requests use the default native tools; the outer flat extension was supplied through explicit CLI flags that the child commands omitted. The parent’s flat requests resume afterward with its prior context preserved. Pinned source and retained command/request/tool-result ordering support a recursive CLI invocation explanation, rather than an established parent compaction switch. Captured OS ancestry, every child setting/binary, original HTTP traffic and the effect of those calls on reward were not proved. This explanation does not repair the protocol failure.

Independent review reproduced the archive/grid joins, counts, bootstrap intervals and both sensitivities. Cost was **26.20 requested H100-hours**, not a utilization or invoice measurement. Native jobs and containers completed; exact GPU Pod absence/provider release has not yet been established. No new run, harness change or training-data promotion follows from this result.
